Core Rules

Draft

Part I: Core Rules

Chapter 1: The Roll

Roll 2d12 and add the relevant Modifier. Compare the total to the DC to find the outcome tier.

Many other effects can add extra dice to the roll.

There are four Attributes: Body, Mind, Appeal and Instinct. They start at 0, and your Species and Class change them when you build your character.

Your Attribute Modifier for an Attribute equals its value: with Body 2, your Body Modifier is +2. Weapon, Power and Signature rolls use their own Modifiers instead (see Chapter 5).

Outcome Tiers

Tier Result Total
Tier 1 Failure Below the DC
Tier 2 Marginal Success From the DC to DC + 6
Tier 3 Full Success DC + 7 or more

A Tier 2 or Tier 3 result is a success; rules that care about it say "when you get a Tier 2 or 3 result." The names of the tiers are flavor: the rules use Tier 1, 2 and 3.

For improvised rolls, such as during roleplay, you don't always need three results: coming up with them every time can take a toll on the GM. When you just want a yes or no, Tier 1 is a failure and Tier 2 or 3 is a success.

Exploding Dice

When a d12 shows a 12, it explodes: count that die as 11, then roll it again and add the result. If the new roll is a 12, it explodes again.

Example

You roll a 12 and a 5. The 12 explodes: you count it as 11 and reroll it, getting an 8. The total is 11 + 8 + 5 = 24, plus your Modifier.

Some damage dice explode the same way. A damage die written with ! (1d6!) explodes: when it shows its highest face, count that face as one less, then roll it again and add the result; it can explode again. A d6! that shows a 6 and then a 4 deals 5 + 4 = 9. Every weapon's die is written with ! (see Weapon Damage [W]); a die with no ! never explodes.

Doubles

If both d12s show the same number (before explosions), the result moves up one tier: Failure becomes Marginal Success, and Marginal Success becomes Full Success. Full Success can't go higher: it becomes a Critical instead (see below).

A Doomed roll can't produce Doubles. On a Favored roll, any two of the three dice that match are Doubles (see Favored and Doomed Rolls).

Critical

A result is a Critical when you roll Doubles on a result that is already Tier 3, when your total is 20 or more above the DC (33 or more against DC 13), or when a Favored roll shows the same number on all three dice. Doubles that raise a Tier 2 to Tier 3 are not a Critical.

A Critical matters for the few Actions that have a Critical row, written under Tier 3 and above the Effects. On a Critical, you get the Tier 3 result and the Critical effect as well. For any other Action, a Critical is simply a Tier 3. Once an encounter, a Critical on one of your Actions also raises your Escalation by 1 (see Escalation).

Boons and Banes

  • Each Boon adds 1 to your total, and each Bane subtracts 1.
  • Boons and Banes cancel each other: 3 Boons and 1 Bane add 2 to your total.

Named Boons and Banes

Some Boons and Banes have a name: Field, Pressure or Support. The rule or Action that gives them writes the name ("1 Field Bane", "1 Support Boon"); a Boon or Bane written without a name has none. Boons with the same name add up to 2, and so do Banes with the same name. Any more of that name add nothing. Boons and Banes without a name always add up.

Name What it is For example
Field Where you and the target are, and how well you see it Cover, Flanking, Prone, Obscured, a Long weapon against an adjacent creature, shooting into a melee
Pressure Banes an effect of another creature puts on you A zone that hinders your Strikes, a blow that leaves you reeling
Support Boons an effect gives several allies at once A war cry for every ally within 5 squares

Apply the limit to each side first, then cancel: 3 Field Banes and 1 Field Boon are 2 Banes and 1 Boon, so 1 Bane.

Five Boons or Banes

After the limits and the cancelling, if you still have 5 or more Boons, you don't add them: the roll is Favored instead. With 5 or more Banes, the roll is Doomed instead. 8 Boons and 3 Banes leave 5 Boons: the roll is Favored. 6 Boons and 2 Banes leave 4 Boons: add 4.

Favored and Doomed Rolls

When a roll is Favored, you roll 3d12 and keep the two highest. If any two of the three dice show the same number (before explosions), you have Doubles, even when one of them is not kept. If all three show the same number, the result is a Critical, whatever the total.

When a roll is Doomed, you roll 3d12 and keep the two lowest. A Doomed roll can't produce Doubles.

A roll that is both Favored and Doomed is a normal roll, and nothing is added to it: 5 Boons that make a Doomed roll Favored leave a normal roll, not a roll with 5 Boons. A roll can't be Favored or Doomed twice.

Roll three dice, then see if there are any explosions, calculated per die.

Example

You are Doomed and roll three different-colored dice: 10 (blue), 12 (green) and 12 (red). You reroll the two 12s and get 10 (green) and 5 (red): green is 11 + 10 = 21 and red is 11 + 5 = 16. You keep the two lowest, blue and red, so your result is 26 (10 + 16), with no Doubles.

Example

You are Favored and roll 1 (blue), 1 (green) and 5 (red). You keep the two highest, a 1 and the 5 (6), and the two 1s are Doubles: the result moves up one tier.

  1. Roll 3d12.
  2. Each die explodes on its own (a 12 counts as 11 and is rolled again; further 12s explode again). After all explosions, each die has its own total.
  3. Keep the two highest totals (Favored) or the two lowest totals (Doomed).
  4. Favored only: if any two of the three dice showed the same face before exploding, you have Doubles; if all three did, a Critical.

Rolls

A Roll is anything you roll. There are six kinds, and every roll is exactly one of them:

Kind What it is
Check One Attribute Modifier against a DC, outside an Action: a "Body Check" (see Checks).
Save A roll to resist something: an "Appeal Save" (see Saves).
Weapon roll An Action with the Weapon trait, and not the Signature or Save trait. It rolls your Weapon Modifier.
Power roll An Action with the Power trait, and not the Signature or Save trait. It rolls your Power Modifier.
Signature roll An Action with the Signature trait. It rolls your Signature Modifier.
Attribute Action Any other Action that rolls: it rolls the Attribute Modifier named by its Body, Mind, Appeal or Instinct trait.

If an Action has multiple traits that reference the type of roll, such as the Trip Basic Action that has both Body and Instinct traits, it is both a Body and Instinct Action, even though you only use one Attribute.

A Split Action is a Weapon roll or a Power roll, depending on the mode you choose when you use it. A [Save] Action doesn't roll: its targets roll Saves (see Save Actions). Damage dice and the Dying and Shattered Tables are not Rolls: nothing that changes a Roll (a Boon, Doomed, Unconscious) changes them.

An effect on Actions names their trait: "1 Boon on [Weapon] Actions" helps every Action with the Weapon trait, whatever Modifier it rolls (a [Signature, Weapon] Action too). An effect that names a Check or a Save applies only to that kind. An effect that names an Attribute and "Rolls" applies to every kind that rolls that Attribute: its Checks, its Saves and its Attribute Actions. Weapon, Power and Signature rolls use no Attribute. "Your Rolls" means all of them.

The effect says Attribute* Check Attribute* Save Attribute* Action Weapon roll Power roll Signature roll
1 Boon on Attribute* Checks ✔ — — — — —
1 Boon on Attribute* Saves — ✔ — — — —
1 Boon on Attribute* Rolls ✔ ✔ ✔ — — —
1 Boon on [Weapon] Actions — — — ✔ — ✔ if it has the Weapon trait
1 Boon on [Power] Actions — — — — ✔ ✔ if it has the Power trait

*Body, Mind, Appeal or Instinct (the same one in each row and column).

Checks

A Check is a roll of one Attribute Modifier against a DC, written "Body Check" or "Instinct Check". The default DC is 13 unless something says otherwise, like "DC 12 Body Check".

Saves

Some effects make a creature roll a Save, written like "Appeal Save: [R] 1d6 / 1d4 / 0 Ho". The creature that must save rolls the named Attribute Modifier against the DC of the effect.

The DC is usually 11 + the Weapon, Power or Signature Modifier that sets it (or 11 + ⌈Attribute ÷ 2⌉ + 1 for an Attribute-based Save); if no DC is listed, it is usually 13.

The three values are what happens on its Tier 1 / Tier 2 / Tier 3 result: here 1d6 Holy Resolve damage on a Tier 1, 1d4 on a Tier 2 and nothing on a Tier 3. Boons, Banes, Doubles, Favored and Doomed work on Saves like on any roll.

Save Actions

An Action with the Save trait doesn't roll: each target rolls the Save the card names (its roll line says, for example, Save: Instinct). The DC comes from the Action's other traits: 11 + your Weapon Modifier for a [Save, Weapon] Action, 11 + your Power Modifier for a [Power, Save] Action, 11 + your Signature Modifier for a [Save, Signature] Action, and for a Save Action that rolls an Attribute (such as [Body, Save]), 11 + ⌈Attribute ÷ 2⌉ + 1. These are your Power DC, your Weapon DC, your Signature DC and the DC of an Attribute (your Body DC): a rule or a card can name one ("an Appeal Save against your Power DC").

The tiers are the target's result: Tier 1 is the worst for them. So everything that follows your result on an attack follows theirs here, reversed: a [Save, Weapon] Action deals its [Mod] on Tier 1 and 2, and a line for two Tiers is written Tier 1 or 2.

A Save Action has no Critical. Boons and Banes on your own rolls don't apply to it; effects on the target's Saves do. Vulnerable gives the target that many Banes on the Save. Cover gives it Field Boons (1 for Low cover, 2 for Medium), and High cover makes its Save Favored, counted from the center of the area's Point of Origin to the target (from your square when the Action has no area). Your Senses don't change a Save Action: the target rolls, so a target that is Obscured or Hidden to you adds no Bane to its Save.

Roll Effects

Each Tier of a roll says what happens: damage, a condition, a movement, healing. This is how the most common effects are written. Conditions are in Conditions, Heal and Rally Points in Rally Points, and Forced Movement in Forced Movement.

Damage on a Card

The damage of an Action is what its card says: it adds a Modifier or a weapon's damage only when the card writes [Mod] or [W]. A Weapon Action writes the weapon's damage and its Modifier on the card; a Power Action writes its dice.

Modifier Damage [Mod]

When an Action deals damage equal to your Modifier, it is written [Mod]. The Modifier is always the one you used to roll for that Action. You never add a Modifier to the same damage twice.

When a Weapon Action adds your Modifier to its damage, the Modifier joins the weapon's damage and keeps its damage type and subtype: if the weapon deals Resolve damage, so does the Modifier. A Tier that writes [Mod] with no [W] deals it as the weapon's damage too, with the weapon's type and subtype.

Power Actions don't add their Modifier to damage on any Tier: their damage is the dice on the card.

Damage Types

All damage a creature takes is either Vigor damage (wounds, bruises, broken bones) or Resolve damage (fear, pain, despair), named after the two thresholds of the Health Pool; each of those has different subtypes. Blunt damage will almost always be Vigor damage, but not always. Damage is written this way:

  • [V]: Vigor damage.
  • [R]: Resolve damage.
  • [C]: the origin chooses which type (Vigor or Resolve) the damage deals.

Vigor and Resolve are not the Body and Mind Attributes: an Action of any Attribute can deal either.

Some Actions include two types of damage. For example, "[V] 1d4+1d6+3 Sl + [R] 1d8 Ps" deals 1d4+1d6+3 Slash Vigor damage and 1d8 Psychic Resolve damage.

Damage Subtypes

Subtypes don't have rules by themselves, but other rules use them, such as Resist and Weak. They are shortened to two letters, so they never look like the damage types [V], [R] and [C]:

Subtype Short Subtype Short Subtype Short
Acid Ac Fire Fi Psychic Ps
Blunt Bl Force Fo Slash Sl
Cold Co Holy Ho Thunder Th
Electricity El Pierce Pi Unholy Un

Resist, Weak and Immune

Some creatures take less, or more, damage of a subtype. It is written on the creature, with a number: Resist 2 Fire, Weak 5 Holy, Immune Fire. A Hatchling might have Resist 2 Fire, a Young dragon Resist 5 and an Ancient one Immune Fire.

  • Each time you take damage from one Action or effect, add up all its damage of that subtype, Vigor and Resolve together, and apply your line once: Resist N reduces the total by N (minimum 0), Weak N adds N. "[V] 1d8 Fi + [R] 5 Fi" against Resist 5 Fire is (1d8 + 5) − 5: one reduction, never one per part.
  • When the damage is split between Vigor and Resolve, the resisting creature chooses which part it reduces first; for Weak, the origin chooses where the extra goes.
  • Immune makes that damage 0.
  • Damage that comes back each turn, such as Lingering, counts each time it lands: Resist 5 Fire stops a Lingering 3 Fi entirely.
  • Two Resists or two Weaks of the same subtype don't add up: the highest applies (see Stacking).

Riders

In a tier cell, what follows the damage is a rider: "[V] 2d8 Pi; Prone" knocks the target Prone on that Tier. A rider happens whatever damage is dealt: Resist, Immune, a damage reduction or Guard can take the damage to 0 (all of it, or one of several damages), and the rider still happens. A Save Action's cells read the same way, each on its own result.

Cleave

When you Cleave N, you deal the Modifier used as damage (with the same damage type and subtype as your weapon) to up to N creatures that are adjacent to the original target.

Several Targets

When one Action affects several creatures (an Area, a Strike on "up to three creatures", or one that says "all creatures"), you roll once, after the targets are chosen (for an Area, after you place it). The dice are shared, but every target is calculated on its own:

  • The DC is calculated against each creature.
  • Each creature has its own Boons, Banes, Favored and Doomed: cover, Prone, Vulnerable, range and so on can apply to one target and not to another.
  • The Tier, Doubles and Critical are decided separately for each creature.
  • Damage is rolled per Tier: once the Action is rolled and you see which creatures landed on which Tier, roll that Tier's damage once and apply it to every creature on that Tier.

For instance, if the Action deals 1d4 / 1d6 / 1d8, and two creatures get Tier 1 and one gets Tier 2, you roll 1d4 once and apply it to the two creatures on Tier 1.

All damage is rolled per die. If the Tier 2 damage of a Save is [V] 1d8 Co + [R] 1d6 Ho, the creature causing the Save rolls both 1d8 and 1d6 and deals that damage to all creatures who got a Tier 2. If the creature causing the Save is Empowered, its 1d6! goes to one creature it damages (see Empowered).

You roll every die that any of the targets needs, and each target uses only the ones that apply to it. If any target has Favored or Doomed, roll 3d12: a Favored target keeps the two highest and has Doubles if any two of the three dice match, a Doomed target keeps the two lowest, and any other target uses the first two d12 you rolled.

Example

You attack Peter and Will with one Action. You have 1 Boon against Will but not against Peter. You roll 2d12 once: Will's total gets +1 and Peter's doesn't.

Example

You attack one Favored target and one non-Favored target with the same Action. You roll 3d12. For the Favored target you keep the two highest, and any pair among the three dice is Doubles. For the other target you use the first two d12 in the order rolled, and only those two can be Doubles.

Rounding

Round up by default. When a rule divides or multiplies a number and the result isn't a whole number, round it up, unless the rule says otherwise.

Reading an Action

Actions are written as cards. Every card has the same structure, from top to bottom:

  1. The name.
  2. Escalation, Frequency and cost, at the right of the name: the Escalation the card needs (if any), its Frequency and its cost in Action Points. A card with no cost says Passive.
  3. The Flavor: one sentence that describes what is done and seen. It is not a rule.
  4. The traits, on a line of their own.
  5. Distance and Area: how far the Action reaches, and the area it affects.
  6. Target: whom it affects.
  7. The roll, as the first line of what the Action does: Attack: Weapon vs. Armor Defense (you roll that Modifier against that Defense) or Save: Appeal (each target rolls that Save).
  8. The Tiers: what happens on each result of the roll. A line can stand for two Tiers ("Tier 1 or 2"); a Tier that isn't written does nothing.
  9. The other lines. Every line of a card has a label that says what it is:
Label What the line is
Requirement What must be true to use the card (see Requirements).
Interrupt, Trigger The moment a [[Reactions
Setup What happens before the rest of the Action (see Setup).
A word in bold (Smite dice, Judged) A word the card defines for its own text.
Effect What happens when the card is used, whatever the roll. Before the roll's line, it happens before the roll; after the Tiers, after them.
Critical An extra result on a Critical, under Tier 3.
Special A rule about the card itself: a limit, an exception, an extra cost.
Passive What a card with no cost does. It works on its own.

The lines are written in the order they happen.

Versions and Modes. Some cards have parts under a heading of their own. A Version is the same Action at another cost: its heading is the cost ("1 AP", "2 AP"), and you pay the cost of the Version you use. A Mode is one of several things the card can do at the same cost: its heading is the Mode's name, followed by the traits only that Mode has, and each time you use the card you choose one Mode. A part has its own lines, and its own Distance and Target when they differ. Lines written above the parts belong to all of them. The card's Frequency counts every use of the card, whichever Version or Mode.

The numbers on the two cards below are the numbers of the list. The first card needs no Escalation and has no Area, so neither is printed; the second has two Versions, and 10 marks the heading of one.

Smite1Encounter · 2 AP2
Holy light gathers on your weapon as the fight wears on, and you bring all of it down in one blow.3
Signature·Weapon·Strike·Divine·Unfailing4
Distance: Weapon5Target: One creature6
Smite dice[R] 1d6! Ho for each Escalation you have, up to 4 dice. Against a Profane creature they are 1d8!s.
Attack7Signature vs. Armor Defense
Tier 18Your Smite dice.
Tier 2[V] 1[W] + [Mod] + your Smite dice.
Tier 3[V] 1[W] + [Mod] + your Smite dice + 1 more Smite die.
Special9When you use Smite, you can spend your Reaction AP to roll 1 more Smite die. Neither extra die counts toward the 4.
Lay On HandsRound · 1 or 2 AP
You stride to an ally's side and lay a hand on them, and a skin of pale light settles over them.
Divine·Focus
Distance: ReachTarget: One willing ally
SetupYou Advance up to 5 squares in a straight line toward the target.
1 AP10
EffectThe target gains Guard equal to 2 + your Power Modifier.
2 AP
EffectThe target gains Guard equal to 2 + your Power Modifier and can use 1 Rally Point.

"As X AP". Some results refer to another cell of the tier table:

  • "As X AP" means the result in the X AP column on the same Tier. So a Tier 2 effect that says "As 2 AP" uses the same effect as the Tier 2 effect of the 2 AP Version.
  • "As X AP, TY" means the result in the X AP column on Tier Y. So a Tier 2 effect that says "As 2 AP, T3" uses the same effect as the Tier 3 effect of the 2 AP Version.
  • "As Tier N" means the result in the same column on Tier N. So a Tier 2 effect that says "As Tier 1" uses the same effect as the Tier 1 effect of this exact Version.
Example

Weapon Attack | At-will · 1 AP
You strike with the weapon in your hands.
Weapon · Strike
Distance: Weapon ✦ Target: One creature
Attack: Weapon vs. Armor Defense
Tier 1: 0
Tier 2: [V] 1[W] + [Mod]
Tier 3: [V] 1[W] + [Mod]

Values written with slashes. Some cards write an entry under the traits once for all their Versions, with one value per Version, in the order of the costs, separated by slashes: One / one / two creatures, 5 / 10 sq., Aura 2 / 3 / 3. Target counts are spelled out in words; distances, areas and other mechanical values use numerals. A distance in squares is written with "sq." (Distance: 5 sq.).

Notation

Written Means
[V], [R], [C] Vigor damage, Resolve damage, or the one the origin chooses. On cards in Foundry, a heart stands for Vigor and a brain for Resolve.
[W] The damage of your weapon.
[Trait] An Action with that trait: "a [Strike] Action", "[Melee] Actions". Several traits in one pair of brackets mean an Action with all of them: "[Ranged, Weapon] Actions".
[Mod] Damage equal to the Modifier used on the roll: your Weapon Modifier on a Weapon roll, your Power Modifier on a Power roll, your Signature Modifier on a Signature roll, or your Attribute Modifier on an Attribute Action.
[HT: …] Hazardous Terrain: written in the text of an effect that creates an area, with its patterns (Entering, Turn, Movement).
Bl, Co, Ho, Pi, Ps, Sl... Damage subtypes, always two letters: Blunt, Cold, Holy, Pierce, Psychic, Slash...
Area: 1 Emanation The area an Action affects, on its own line. A Distance line says how far away it can be placed.
Distance: Weapon The Range of the weapon you use for the Action. Distance: Reach is your Reach.
EoT Until the end of the turn of the affected creature.
(T2/T3) The effect only happens on those tiers.
Critical An extra effect on Doubles with a result that is already Tier 3, or a total 20 or more above the DC.
Evade 2, Advance 2, Pushed 2, Pulled 2, Slid 2, Reposition 2 Movement of up to that many squares.
for 2 rounds How long an effect lasts.
Attack: Body vs. Body The Modifier you roll, and the Defense of the target.
Save: Instinct The Save each target rolls.
(1 round) After a condition or an effect: it lasts 1 round.
0 AP An Action that costs no AP. You can use it only on your turn.
Weapon Attack (1A), (1A/2A) A Linked Action and the Version you use (or a choice of two).
1R, 0R A Reaction that uses 1 AP, or none (which AP can pay: see Reactions).
Escalation 4 The Escalation an Action needs: you can use it only while your Escalation is at least that number. Nothing is spent.

Rules Language

A single creature is referred to as they: "the creature is Hindered until they use a Move Action."

Allies. Your allies are the creatures on your side. You are never your own ally.

Origin. The origin of an effect is the creature that uses the Action, or the Point of Origin of an Area. When a rule says "the origin chooses", the origin decides, not the creature affected.

Since your last turn, this turn. A feature that says "since your last turn" counts from the end of your last turn. "This turn" is the turn in progress, whoever's it is: on your turn, it counts from the start of your turn; on another creature's turn (a Reaction), from the start of that turn.

Up to. A number of things you can use, gain or move is a maximum: you can use fewer, or none, unless the rule says you must. "The target can use 2 Rally Points" lets them use 0, 1 or 2.

Specific beats general. When a card or a feature says something different from a general rule, the card or feature wins for that case. The Evade Action, for example, doesn't trigger Reactions although movement normally does.

When a rule names a trait before the word "Action," it means an Action with that trait. For example, a Divine Action is an Action with the Divine trait. The same goes for a Weapon Action, a Power Action or a Nonlethal Action.

  • Traits inside one pair of square brackets, such as [Ranged, Strike, Weapon] Action, mean an Action with all of those traits: [Trait A, Trait B] is Trait A and Trait B. It doesn't mean only, it just must include the trait: a [Melee] Weapon Attack (1A) is the Weapon Attack Action that uses 1 AP and has the Melee trait, so it doesn't apply to a [Ranged] Weapon Attack (1A).
  • Separate brackets joined by "and" mean either: "[Strike] and [Weapon] Actions" are Actions with the Strike trait, the Weapon trait, or both. Alternatives can also be written with "or" inside the brackets: [Melee or Ranged].
  • A Body Action is an Action with the Body trait, and so on; an Action can be more than one (Trip is both a Body and an Instinct Action).

Weapons by property. When a rule names a weapon property before the word "weapon," it means a weapon with that property. A Two-handed weapon is a weapon with the Two-handed property, and a Projectile weapon is a weapon with the Projectile property, such as a bow or a crossbow.

Summary

  1. Roll 2d12 and add the relevant Modifier.
  2. Any 12 counts as 11 and is rolled again, adding the result.
  3. Add 1 for each Boon and subtract 1 for each Bane. Named ones (Field, Pressure, Support) count up to 2 of each name. If 5 or more Boons are left after cancelling, the roll is Favored instead; 5 or more Banes, Doomed.
  4. Compare to the DC: below it is a Failure, from the DC up to DC + 6 is a Marginal Success, and DC + 7 or more is a Full Success.
  5. If both d12s match, move the result up one tier.
  6. A Favored roll is 3d12: keep the two highest, and any pair among the three is Doubles. A Doomed roll is 3d12: keep the two lowest, with no Doubles.

Chapter 2: Turns and Actions

Encounters

An encounter is a fight or a similar scene: it starts when Initiative is rolled and ends when the GM says it's over. It can't end while a creature is Dying or Shattered: every creature must be unharmed, stabilized or dead. If a creature becomes Dying or Shattered outside of an encounter, it rolls on the Dying or Shattered Table, then Initiative is rolled and that creature goes last.

Designer's Tip

Sometimes, rolling Initiative when a single creature becomes Dying or Shattered and there is no obvious danger around, and an ally can stabilize them easily, is just going to slow down the game. In these non-threatening situations, feel free to roll on the Dying or Shattered Table once, and then the creature stabilizes.

Initiative

At the start of combat, every creature rolls Initiative. Initiative is a Check, normally an Instinct Check, but the GM can call for a different Attribute, for everyone or for some creatures only. The total is the creature's initiative.

Initiative is a zipper. The creatures are split into however many different groups exist. Usually it is the PCs against a single group of enemies, but three-way combat is possible. Each group puts its creatures in order from the highest result to the lowest. The group with the highest single result goes first. Then the groups take turns, one creature at a time, in the order of their highest result, each taking its highest remaining creature. A group with no creatures left is skipped.

Example

Victor rolls 14, Paul 13, Wes 10, Goblin Warrior 12 and Goblin Scoundrel 10. The PCs' highest result is 14 and the enemies' is 12, so the order is: Victor, Goblin Warrior, Paul, Goblin Scoundrel, Wes.

In a three-way fight, Mark rolls 13 and Nick 9, the enemies Goblin Warrior 12 and Goblin Scoundrel 8, and a third group Kobold Mage 13 and Kobold Shaman 5. The order is Mark, Kobold Mage, Goblin Warrior, Nick, Kobold Shaman, Goblin Scoundrel.

Ties are broken by the higher Attribute Modifier used for the Initiative roll. If they are still tied, the Friendly creature (a PC or an ally of the PCs) goes first.

The Start of the Encounter

Some abilities happen at the start of an encounter, such as the Paladin's Judge. After Initiative is rolled and before the first turn, each of them waits in a stack, in the turn order. The GM can change that order: an ally can go later, for example to act after another ally's ability. Then they resolve one at a time, in the stack's order, and the first turn begins.

Example

Chris and Krysta are Paladins. Chris rolls 15 and Krysta 13, so the stack is Chris's Judge, then Krysta's. Chris wants to know which enemy Krysta Judges before choosing his own, so the GM puts Krysta's first.

Swapping Initiative

On your turn, if you haven't taken any Actions yet and aren't Down, you can spend 1 AP to swap places in the turn order with an ally who hasn't had a turn this round. The ally takes the turn now, at your place in the order, and gains its AP as normal.

You act at the ally's old place. Until then, your remaining Actions are frozen: you can't use them. When your new turn arrives, you carry on with the AP you had left instead of gaining new AP. You can't swap again that round.

Example

PC1 (first in the order) swaps with PC3 and keeps 3 AP. The order becomes PC3, NPC1, PC2, NPC2, PC1. When PC1's turn comes, PC1 has 3 AP.

Turns and Rounds

A turn is the time one creature acts, from the start of their turn to the end of it. A round is one full cycle of turns. Limits that say "per turn" count each turn separately, including other creatures' turns: you can make up to 3 Strikes in your turn, and up to 3 more (as reactions) in another creature's turn.

A turn-cycle is the period from the start of a creature's turn to the start of that creature's next turn. In the order "Victor, Goblin Warrior, Paul, Goblin Scoundrel, Wes", Wes's turn-cycle runs from the start of Wes's turn to the start of Wes's next turn.

Action Points

At the start of your turn in combat, you regain AP: you lose any AP you didn't use and gain 4 Action Points (AP) and 1 Reaction AP. You spend AP to do things on your turn. The Reaction AP pays only for Reactions, on your turn or another creature's.

Unspent AP

If you end your turn without spending all your AP, you keep the rest until your next turn starts: nothing else happens then, and those AP can still pay for Reactions. When you regain AP at the start of your next turn, each AP you still had unused gives you Guard for 1 round: 2 per AP at Stages 0 and 1, 3 at Stage 2 and 4 at Stage 3 (see Stages).

  • This Guard adds to any Guard you already have (an exception to Stacking), and what is left of it ends 1 round later, when you regain AP again. Damage takes it before your other Guard.
  • A kept AP you spend on a Reaction is one AP less when your turn starts, so it gives no Guard.
  • Your Reaction AP never becomes Guard, and your first turn of an encounter has no unused AP.
Example

Drak (Stage 0) has Guard 5 from a card and ends his turn with 1 AP left: nothing changes until his next turn (he could still spend that AP on a Reaction). When his next turn starts, he regains his AP and gains Guard 2 for 1 round, on top of his Guard 5: Guard 7. A goblin then hits him for 3: his Guard from AP takes 2 and his other Guard 1, so he has Guard 4 left.

Losing and Gaining Action Points

When something gives or takes Action Points, it says whether it happens now or when you regain AP.

  • Now. "The target loses 1 AP" means they lose 1 AP they have right now; if they have none, it has no effect. "The target gains 1 AP" means they gain 1 AP right now. Unless otherwise stated, you can't have more than 4 AP, and losing or gaining AP never changes your Reaction AP.
  • When you regain AP. Changes to the AP you regain at the start of your turn are the Slowed and Quickened conditions: Slowed 1 means you regain 1 AP less, Quickened 1 means you regain 1 AP more. Neither changes your Reaction AP.

Reactions

A Reaction is an Action you use in response to something another creature does. Its card has an Interrupt or a Trigger line that says what it responds to, and which of the two it is decides when it happens. Its cost is written with an R, such as 1R: it uses that many Action Points, but only as a response. A 0R Reaction uses no AP; its Frequency still limits it.

  • Paying: A Reaction is paid with your Reaction AP, with AP you kept from your turn (see Unspent AP), or with both: a 2R Reaction can use your Reaction AP and one kept AP. On your own turn, your turn's AP can pay for it too. Your Reaction AP lasts until you regain AP at the start of your next turn. A feature can give you a second Reaction AP: it follows the same rules, and the feature says what it can pay for.
  • No Reaction by default: No creature has a Reaction of its own: every Reaction comes from a class, an item or a creature's entry. Moving away from an enemy doesn't let it attack you, unless it has a Reaction that says so.
  • Interrupt: An Interrupt happens before the Action that triggers it. "Interrupt: A creature would Advance" means the Reaction happens before the creature uses the Advance Action. An Interrupt can say that part of its effect happens after the triggering Action ("after the damage, they are Slid 1"): that part waits for it. An Interrupt on a creature that would damage someone happens once the triggering Action's roll is made and its damage is known, before that damage is dealt: the Reaction can't change that roll.
  • Trigger: A Trigger happens after the Action that triggers it. "Trigger: A creature deals damage to you" happens after you take the triggering damage.
  • Once per triggering Action: You can react only once to the same Action, but several creatures can react to it. Some Actions, mainly Move Actions, can happen throughout different squares. It is still a single Action, and you decide when you take the Reaction: for instance, you can wait for the creature to move into a more advantageous position before taking your Reaction, instead of taking it as soon as the creature moves.
  • Multiple creatures reacting to the same trigger, at the same time: You must decide to react before making the rolls: when a creature triggers a Reaction from several creatures, they all decide whether they will react before making any rolls. The creatures taking the Reactions decide the order; if they are opposed, the GM decides or asks for a simple Check to decide who goes first, similar to how Initiative is rolled. If the triggering creature becomes an invalid target after a creature reacts (such as being killed), the remaining creatures still lose the AP as if they had used the Reaction.
  • On any turn: A Reaction can happen during any turn, including your own: if another creature's Action moves them away from you during your turn, you can react to that.
  • You can't use an Action outside your turn unless it is a Reaction.

What a Reaction Responds To

An Interrupt or a Trigger names a moment the rules define, and the Action that holds the moment is the triggering Action. The moments cards use: a creature would leave a square during a Move Action, or uses the Stand Action; an enemy would enter a square adjacent to you or to an ally; an enemy moves closer to you (see Moving Closer); a creature would be moved by Forced Movement, or would fall Prone; a creature moves away from you (see Moving Away); a creature makes a [Strike] Action, or would damage someone; a creature would use a [Power] Action; a creature scores a Tier 3 or a Critical; an ally or an enemy becomes Bloodied or Strained; a creature goes Down; a creature uses a Rally Point; a creature Charges, or enters a square from which it Flanks you. A card can name another moment, as long as the rules define when it happens: "ends a Move Action" is not one.

While the name "triggering" is similar to "Trigger", it isn't only for Trigger Reactions: it also applies to Interrupt Reactions. The triggering creature is the creature who caused the Reaction to happen; the triggering Action is the Action that caused the Reaction to happen, and so on.

Designer's Tip

The clarification above might make you think you need to move one square at a time during a game, but this slows the game down a lot. You can just make the full movement and let the creature reacting decide when it happens during the movement. You might need to move the token back to where the Reaction happened if the movement is disrupted (see below), but that doesn't happen often. Doing it this way removes the suspense of "When will this creature start moving? Should I use my Reaction now, or wait and see if it moves into a more favorable position, with the chance that it stops moving before I react?" The table should decide how to run it.

A Reaction's Target

Every Reaction has a Target line, and its Interrupt or Trigger is written about the target. The creature whose Action sets the Reaction off is the triggering creature.

To use a Reaction you need Line of Effect to its target, as for every Action. You must also perceive the target and the triggering creature (see Senses): Hidden is enough; Unsensed is not.

A Reaction can also do something to the triggering creature when it isn't the target: Shield of Faith's target is the ally, and it Taunts the attacker. That needs Line of Effect to the triggering creature too, like anything a card does to a creature (see Targets of Effects); without it, that part doesn't happen and the rest does.

A feature that says "when..." waits for a moment: you must perceive the creatures it names. What it then does to a creature needs Line of Effect like anything else.

Example

Zack, a Paladin, has Shield of Faith: "Target: One ally. Interrupt: An enemy's [Strike] Action would damage the target." An orc around a corner from Zack shoots Nari, who stands 3 squares from Zack in the open. Zack has Line of Effect to Nari and hears the orc: he uses Shield of Faith, and Nari's damage is reduced. He has no Line of Effect to the orc, so the orc isn't Taunted. Had Nari been the one behind the wall, Zack couldn't have used it at all.

Example

Zack has Rebuke: "Target: One enemy. Trigger: The target moves away from you." A goblin 2 squares from him, on the other side of a wall, runs off. Zack hears it, but Rebuke targets the goblin and he has no Line of Effect to it: he can't use Rebuke.

Example

Zack has Kindled Wrath: "when an ally becomes Bloodied or goes Down, your Escalation increases by 1". Nari becomes Bloodied behind a wall, 6 squares from Zack. Zack hears him (within 10 squares), and Kindled Wrath does nothing to Nari, so it needs no Line of Effect: his Escalation increases. At 12 squares behind that wall, out of sight and hearing, it wouldn't.

Disrupting Actions

When an Action is disrupted, it doesn't happen, and the resources and AP spent on it are wasted. Some Actions can disrupt another Action, usually with a Critical.

An Interrupt disrupts the Action before it happens. For example, a Reaction with "Interrupt: A creature uses a Move Action" triggers when a creature uses an Action that Stands and then Advances (1 AP): the creature doesn't Stand, and the whole Action is disrupted (because you can't Advance while Prone).

A Trigger that names a Move Action fires at any point during the Move Action (after the first square it moves), but it is a single trigger: you can use the Reaction only once per Move Action, even with AP to spare. If the Action does something before moving (Stand, then Advance), the Stand happens first; the Trigger fires during the Advance.

When the disrupted Action is only a Linked Action, the Action stops only if that part is necessary for it. What already happened stays, and a disrupted movement ends in the square the creature was in. For example, a Charge disrupted before the creature has moved the 3 squares it needs is cancelled, and they make no Weapon Attack. If it is disrupted after those 3 squares, the Charge ends there, and they make the Weapon Attack if there is a valid target.

Moving Closer

A creature moves closer to you when the distance between you, counted in squares (every second diagonal counts as 2, as always), is smaller after their movement than before. An Interrupt checks this before the creature enters the square; a Trigger checks it if the creature entered any square nearer to you during the movement. The creature moves closer when it would enter a square that is nearer to you than the square it came from. A step to the side that leaves the distance the same is not closer. Evade, Forced Movement and Reposition don't trigger Reactions, so a Reaction to a creature moving closer can't react to any of them.

Moving Away

A creature moves away from you when the distance between you, counted the same way, is larger after their movement than before. Everything else mirrors Moving Closer:

  • An Interrupt checks before the creature enters the farther square; a Trigger checks whether it entered any square farther from you during the movement.
  • A step that leaves the distance the same is neither closer nor away.
  • A movement that comes closer and then goes away (a creature running past you) moves away from its first farther square.
  • For a creature larger than one square, count from its nearest square to your nearest square.
  • "Within 3 squares of you" on such a Reaction is checked in the square the creature is in when you take the Reaction.
  • If the movement is disrupted, it ends in the square the creature was in when the Reaction was taken.
  • Evade, Forced Movement and Reposition don't trigger Reactions, so they are never "moving away".

Y is you. Blue and orange squares are the squares G enters, in order from G; the number in each is its distance from you.

Actions

An Action is something you spend AP on. Every Action is written as a card; see Reading an Action.

Actions that roll have three tiers.

Whenever an Action is mentioned in the rules, its traits appear next to it. For example, in "You must use 1 AP [Move] to get up from Prone," Move is a trait.

Setup

Some Actions have a Setup line. It says what happens before the rest of the Action.

  • A Setup is optional, unless it says you must. You can do part of it: "You Advance up to 5 squares" lets you move fewer, or not at all.
  • The Action's Distance and its targets are checked after the Setup. You can start out of reach, and the Setup brings you there. If no valid target is within the Distance after the Setup, the rest of the Action doesn't happen, and its cost is still paid.
  • A Setup that names the Action's target fixes it. If the Setup says "toward the target", you choose that target before the Setup, and it stays the Action's target.
  • If an Action in your Setup is disrupted, the rest of the Action still happens. Only then, if the Setup had named a target, you can choose another target for the rest of the Action.
  • Setups don't stack. When something gives a Setup to an Action that already has one, you choose which of the two Setups to use.

Targets

An Action that targets something can only be used if it has a valid target. An Action with no valid target can't be used. An Action that names a number of targets needs that many: "Two creatures" can't be used against one. "Up to" means any number from one to that many. Most Actions target creatures only, but the GM can allow one to target an unattended object, such as a barrel, a crate or a door. Usually the Action rolls against DC 13 for the object, but the GM can set a different DC depending on the circumstances.

Willing and Unwilling

Some Actions target a willing creature, and some rules change for an unwilling one (passing through its square, for example). A creature is willing when it accepts the effect: you choose for yourself, and each creature chooses for itself when the effect would happen. An Unconscious creature counts as willing. Any other creature that doesn't accept is unwilling. A creature doesn't have to know what the effect does to accept it.

Requirements

Some Actions have Requirements, written under the Frequency line (and above the Interrupt or Trigger of a Reaction). To use the Action, you must meet them; otherwise you can't use it at all. They are checked when you start to use the Action, before you pay its cost and before any Setup. Charge requires at least Speed 3: with Speed 2, you can't Charge, and a Speed bonus that the Charge itself gives doesn't count toward it.

0 AP Actions

A 0 AP Action costs no AP, but it is still an Action: you can use it only on your turn, and its Frequency still limits it. An Action that costs no AP and is used in response to something is a Reaction, written 0R (see Reactions). Linked Actions cost no AP either, because they are part of another Action.

Linked Actions

An Action that another Action lets you use as part of it is a Linked Action. It is written with the AP of the Version you use, such as "Weapon Attack (1A)", or "(1A/2A)" when you choose between two Versions.

  • It is part of the original Action, so it costs no AP.
  • It keeps its traits and requirements, unless the Action says otherwise: you must still be able to use it. If an Action lets you Evade (a Linked Action) while you are Immobilized, you can't.
  • It affects the target of the original Action, unless it says otherwise. If the original Action doesn't list a target, you can choose the target per Linked Action.
  • It doesn't count toward its own uses: not toward its Frequency, the 3 Strikes of the turn, or At-will Banes, unless the Action says otherwise (a Charge's Weapon Attack counts toward At-will Banes).
  • If it isn't optional and you can't make it, the whole Action is disrupted, except for a movement (below). A Linked Action is optional when the Action says you can make it ("you can Evade 2"), and required when it says you do it ("you Advance 5, make a Weapon Attack (1A) and Advance 5 again").
  • A movement you can't make. When an Action has you move ("You Evade 2") and you can't (you are Immobilized or Prone, or no square is open to you), you move 0 squares and the rest of the Action happens. If the Action says you must move ("you must Evade 2 first"), the movement is necessary: the whole Action is disrupted.

If a Linked Action has no valid target, the rest of the Action is disrupted (that Linked Action and anything after it don't happen); what already happened stays. By default, you can't change the target of a Linked Action. For example, if a player asks to change the target from a creature to an object so they can continue the Action, the GM should probably accept it only if it makes sense, such as attacking a door on the way, and not "attacking the ground".

Example

The Archer's Opening Shot lets an ally make a Weapon Attack (1A). On that ally's own turn they can still use Weapon Attack as its own Action, and that first use has no At-will Bane.

Targets of Effects

Unless something says otherwise, the effects of an Action, and the Actions it lets you use (Linked Actions), affect the target of the Action. Remember, if the Action doesn't have a target, you choose who to target on each individual Linked Action. If you use Shove on an enemy, the enemy is the one who is Pushed.

Line of Effect, always. Whatever a card or a feature does to a creature (damages it, moves it, heals it, gives it a condition, Guard, a Boon or a Bane, or lets it act), you need Line of Effect to that creature at that moment, whether the creature is on the Target line or named in the text. In an Area, the line is from the Point of Origin. A creature you have no Line of Effect to isn't affected; the rest of the card still happens. A card that works without it says so: "(no Line of Effect needed)".

An effect on one creature that others gain or lose from (Vulnerable, Taunted, a creature made easier to perceive) is done to that creature alone: you need no Line of Effect to the others.

Effect Timing

Every line of a card says when it happens (see Reading an Action):

  • A Tier line happens only on that Tier. A line for two Tiers says so: "Tier 1 or 2". A Tier that isn't written does nothing.
  • An Effect line happens whenever the card is used, whatever the roll. Before the roll's line, it happens before the roll; after the Tiers, after them.
  • Actions with no roll have no Tiers: their Effect simply happens.

Inside a Tier's line, the damage is written first and applied first; what follows the semicolon happens after the damage is applied ("[V] 1[W] + [Mod]; Prone").

Some cards mark an effect for some Tiers only, with the Tiers in parentheses: "Immobilized (T3)" is only Immobilized on a Tier 3 result, and "(T2/T3)" is Tier 2 or Tier 3.

Buffs

A Buff is an effect that modifies another Action, such as One More Arrow's 1[W] more on one of your [Strike] Actions.

  • A Buff that gives a single value ("+[R] 1d6 Co") applies on every Tier, Tier 1 included.
  • A Buff that gives a value per Tier ("+[R] 1d4/1d6/1d8 Co") applies its Tier 1 value on a Tier 1, its Tier 2 value on a Tier 2 and its Tier 3 value on a Tier 3.
  • A Buff that only applies from Tier 2 onward is written with a 0 on Tier 1: "+[R] 0/1d6/1d8 Co".
  • On an Action with several targets, a Buff or a Debuff is rolled once per Tier, not per creature (see Several Targets).

Raising Defenses. "+1 Defense" raises every Defense of the creature: Armor Defense, Ward Defense and every Vs. Attribute. "+1 AD", "+1 WD" or "+1 Defense vs Body" raises only that one. A feature can narrow it further, such as "+1 Defense vs Actions that Push". These bonuses don't add up with each other (see Stacking).

Stacking

Unless a card says otherwise, the same effect never stacks with itself, and bonuses from different effects don't add up either: for each value (Vulnerable, Slowed, a Defense, Guard...), a creature uses only the highest bonus and the highest penalty that apply. If a creature gets the same effect again, it keeps the higher value and the longer duration: two effects that make it Vulnerable 1 do not make it Vulnerable 2. A condition with a source, such as Frightened of a creature, comes from one source at a time (see Chapter 8: Conditions).

Five things do add up:

  • An effect that says it increases a value: "increase your Slowed value by 1" adds to the Slowed you have.
  • Boons and Banes, up to the limit of their name (see Named Boons and Banes).
  • Named bonuses. A bonus to a value such as a Defense or a Speed can have a name, as Boons and Banes do: Field, Pressure or Support. Bonuses with different names add up; with the same name, only the highest counts. An unnamed bonus never adds to another bonus: it counts only when it is higher than the named ones together.
  • An effect that increases your Slowed value (being Desperate, Dying or Shattered).
  • The Guard your Unspent AP give you: it adds to the Guard you have.

For example, Jacob has a +1 Support bonus to every Defense and a +1 Field bonus to Armor Defense: his Armor Defense rises by 2. A second +1 Support bonus changes nothing, and an unnamed +1 bonus doesn't add to them either: he keeps +2.

A card can say otherwise. Judge does: multiple Paladins can Judge the same creature. For example, Chris and Krysta are Paladins and both Judge the same Orc. It is Judged by Chris and Judged by Krysta: it counts as Profane for each of them, and each of them can reduce its damage once each round.

Equipment is not a bonus. Your armor gives your Armor value and your charm your Ward value; effects add to those. With +1 AD and +1 Defense, your Armor Defense rises by 1 (not 2) and every other Defense by 1.

Example

Weight of Judgment reduces the Speed of a creature a Paladin Judged by 2. If two Paladins with it Judge the same creature, its Speed is still reduced by 2, not 4: it is the same effect.

Frequency

Some Actions have a Frequency, written in the title bar of the card, such as At-will, Turn (once per turn), Round (once per round), Encounter (once per encounter) or Daily (once per Sleep). Actions with no Frequency can be used as often as you have AP.

Some traits can change the Frequency or expand the Frequency rules, such as the Strike trait, which limits you to a maximum of three Strikes per turn (see Chapter 7).

At-will

An At-will Action can be used any number of times, but each use after the first in a turn adds 1 Bane to the roll. For example, if you use Weapon Attack three times in one turn, the first roll is normal, the second has 1 Bane, and the third has 2 Banes. This doesn't apply to Linked Actions.

Each use after the first in a turn adds 1 Bane per specific At-will Action. Different At-will Actions each have their own first-use count.

On an Action with no roll, At-will has no mechanical effect: it is a stylistic default for Actions that can be used freely on your turn.

Turn

A Turn Action can be used once per turn: once on your turn, and once on each other creature's turn, as long as you have the AP. A Reaction with the Turn Frequency can answer one creature on its turn and another on theirs.

Round

A Round Action can be used once per turn-cycle, not once per round number: if you are at the end of the Initiative order, use a Round Action, end your turn and a new round begins, you still can't use it again until your whole turn-cycle completes. A card that says "once a round" or "once each round" means the same: once per turn-cycle.

Encounter

An Encounter Action can be used once during a whole encounter. It resets when the encounter ends, which is the GM's call.

Daily

A Daily Action can be used once, and again only after you complete a Sleep.

Versus

An Action that rolls uses a Modifier and, if it targets a creature, rolls against a Defense or DC. The Modifier is your Weapon, Power, Signature or Attribute Modifier (see Chapter 5). Every Action that rolls says so on its Attack line, which names the Modifier and the Defense: "Attack: Weapon vs. Armor Defense". The Defense is Armor Defense (AD), Ward Defense (WD), an Attribute ("vs. Body") or a specific DC.

Defenses

An Action against a creature rolls against one of its Defenses. A creature has three kinds:

Defense DC
Armor Defense (AD) the creature's Armor Defense
Ward Defense (WD) the creature's Ward Defense
Vs. an Attribute 12 + the target's Attribute
Vs. DC A set DC, such as "Vs. DC 13": some Actions have a set DC, and others target something that has no Defenses, such as a stationary object.
  • Armor value is the value provided by the armor a creature wears. Armor Defense is 11 + Armor value + other items + bonuses − penalties.
  • Ward value is the value provided by the ward a creature carries or is, such as a holy symbol, a charm, a ring or a feature. Ward Defense is 11 + your Power Modifier + Ward value + other items + bonuses − penalties. A creature without a ward normally has Ward value 0; items and features can increase this value.

Rounds and Durations

Until

When an effect says it lasts until something happens, it lasts through that something, and ends once it has been resolved. For example, a creature that is Hindered until they use a Move Action is still Hindered during that Move Action, and stops being Hindered afterwards. "Until you leave your square" ends after any movement, Forced Movement and Reposition included (see Moving and Leaving Your Square).

Your Next Action

When an Action says an effect happens on your next Action and gives no duration (unlike "For 1 round"), you must make that Action before the end of your current turn. If you don't, the effect is wasted.

When an effect gives another creature its next roll or its next Action ("its next roll has 1 Boon"), it lasts until that creature makes one. It is wasted if the creature hasn't made one by the end of its next turn (given during that creature's own turn, by the end of that turn).

Rounds

A round is one full cycle of turns. It starts with the first creature's turn and ends when the last creature ends their turn.

An effect that lasts a number of rounds counts down by 1 at the end of the initiative slot in which it was applied (the origin's own slot when it was applied on its turn, the current slot when it was applied as a Reaction or out of turn), starting with that slot's next turn: the end of the turn in which it was applied doesn't count. An effect that lasts 2 rounds is written "for 2 rounds", or with the rounds in parentheses after it: "Taunted by you (1 round)". A duration is one of these: EoT; a number of rounds; "until the encounter ends"; until a Save ends it; or a condition's own end (Prone lasts until you Stand). Nothing lasts "until the start of your next turn".

Example

On the first round of combat, Victor (the first creature in the turn order) causes an effect on Wes that lasts 2 rounds. The effect ends at the end of Victor's turn on the third round.

End of Turn

When an effect lasts until the end of the turn of the affected creature, it is marked EoT.

An EoT effect on yourself still ends at the end of the current turn. A duration in rounds is different: it does not count down at the end of the turn in which the effect was created, because it has to last a whole round.

Each position in the turn order is an initiative slot. Effects end at the end of an initiative slot, not of a creature. If a creature swaps initiative, an EoT effect still ends at the end of the slot the creature was in when the effect was applied, and a duration in rounds counts down at the end of the slot in which the effect was applied (the origin's own slot when it was applied on its turn, the current slot when it was applied as a Reaction or out of turn).

Escalation

Escalation is a character's adrenaline: a level from 1 to 6 that rises as a fight goes on. Each PC has their own. It is never spent: your class's Escalation abilities work while your Escalation is high enough.

  • Start: you start every encounter at Escalation 1 + your party's Momentum.
  • Rounds: at the start of every round after the first, if you aren't Unconscious, your Escalation increases by 1. While Unconscious, you keep the Escalation you have.
  • Critical: once an encounter, when you score a Critical on one of your Actions, your Escalation increases by 1.
  • Your class's hook: each class names one more event that, once an encounter, increases your Escalation by 1 (the Paladin: an ally becomes Bloodied or goes Down; the Archer: an enemy you have damaged goes Down). You gain your class's hook at level 2.
  • At most 6: you can't have more than 6 Escalation, unless a feature says so. A Critical or a hook that happens while your Escalation is already 6 does nothing, and it isn't used up for the encounter.
  • The end: when the encounter ends, your Escalation goes back to 1, and the abilities that need it stop working.

Your class has two kinds of Escalation abilities (see Escalation Abilities):

  • Escalation abilities, at Escalation 2, 4 and 6: a Passive works while your Escalation is at least its number ("while your Escalation is 4 or more"); an Action whose card says Escalation N can be used only then (Reckoning, Escalation 6). You gain them one level at a time (see Leveling Up).
  • The Apex: an Encounter Action whose card says Escalation 6. You can use it only while your Escalation is 6; it spends nothing. It comes at level 4, the first level of Stage 1.

An Action with an Escalation line on its card needs that much Escalation, the same way.

Example

Nari's party has Momentum 1, so he starts a fight at Escalation 2: his Escalation 2 Passive works from his first turn. Round 2 starts: he is at 3. In round 2 he scores a Critical: he is at 4, and his Escalation 4 Passive starts working. Round 3 starts: 5. Round 4: 6, and he stays there. When the fight ends, he is back at 1.

NPCs have no Escalation, except Elites (see Elite Escalation).

Momentum

Momentum is the edge your party builds over an expedition: a number from 0 to 4 that the whole party shares. Each of you starts an encounter at Escalation 1 + Momentum, so at 5 at most.

  • Gaining: +1 after each encounter the party overcomes: a fight, a negotiation, a sneak, a Challenge.
  • Losing: -1 each time a PC goes Down, and -1 at each Sleep. If the party retreats from an encounter, it loses all of it.
  • A Rest clears it: you leave a Rest with Momentum 0.
  • It is never under 0 or above 4.
Example

Jacob's party has Momentum 2 after two fights, so the third starts at Escalation 3. In it Jacob goes Down: Momentum 1. They win: Momentum 2 again. They sleep in the ruins: 1 in the morning.

Designer's Tip

The GM's valve: after a bad turn of the dice for the whole table, the GM can give every PC +1 Escalation. It is the only raise outside the rules above, and nothing spends Escalation.

Chapter 3: Movement and the Environment

Playing on the Grid

Fights are played on a map divided into squares, on a table or in a virtual tabletop. Every creature is a token that stands on one or more squares, and every distance in these rules is counted in squares.

You move around the grid using Actions. Some allow you to move up to your Speed (like Advance); others have special rules, like the Evade Action, which lets you move without triggering Reactions.

When calculating distances and movement, each square counts as 1, but every second diagonal counts as 2 squares (1, 2, 1, 2...). Areas and ranges are measured the same way. Exception: Forced Movement and Reposition count each diagonal square as 1 (see Forced Movement and Reposition). If you are calculating your movement on your turn, the count continues through your whole turn, across every Action that moves you. If you move when it isn't your turn, you calculate it from the start: you don't keep track of the movement from your previous turn.

  • Counting squares: count the squares from one creature to the other, not the one they stand on. A creature next to you, even diagonally, is 1 square away.
  • Elevation: count the squares up or down as you count the squares on the map, then add them together like a diagonal: the larger count, plus half the smaller one (rounded down). A creature 4 squares away and 4 squares up is 6 squares away. How tall a creature is: see Size.

Size

Every creature has a Size: a rank from 1 to 7, its SR (Size Rank), written with its name first, such as Medium (3). Size says how many squares a creature occupies, and it is used to compare creatures.

Size Rank Occupies Squares
Tiny 1 1 × 1 1
Small 2 1 × 1 1
Medium 3 1 × 1 1
Large 4 2 × 2 4
Huge 5 3 × 3 9
Gargantuan 6 4 × 4 16
Titanic 7 5 × 5 25

The side of the area a creature occupies is its rank minus 2, and at least 1. An Action can compare SR: "The target's SR is at most 1 higher than yours" means the target's rank is no more than one above yours. Any smaller creature qualifies.

A creature is as tall as it is wide: one that occupies more than one square also occupies more squares height-wise, so imagine it as a cube. A Large creature (2 × 2) is 2 squares tall, and a Gargantuan one (4 × 4) is 4 squares tall. This might feel odd for some creatures, such as a horse, but the simplification is necessary for the game to work.

Size doesn't change Reach by itself: a Large creature still has Reach 1. Anything that makes a creature bigger says whether its Reach changes too.

Squeezing

Creatures can normally squeeze to reach places smaller than themselves, but not to the point that wouldn't make sense. A creature can squeeze through a space one rank below theirs (a Large creature, 2 × 2, can squeeze through a gap 1 square wide), and each square they move this way counts as Difficult Terrain. If a creature stops moving while squeezing to do another Action, meaning they don't fit completely in the space they are in, all their Rolls are Doomed and they are Vulnerable equal to half their level (rounded up) until they move to a space where they fit completely. Some creatures have features that change this, like a Gargantuan (4 × 4) snake with "The snake can squeeze through 1 square", but this doesn't mean the creature can safely end its turn while squeezing: unless otherwise noted, the Doomed penalty and the Vulnerable condition above still apply.

Forced Movement and Reposition never squeeze a creature: they stop in the last square where it fits completely (see Collision).

Movement

An Action that lets you move gives a distance, written "Advance 5" or "Evade 2". You can always move less than the specified amount: "Advance 5" means up to 5 squares, not exactly 5. But each time you move with an Action, you can't move more than your current Speed, unless an ability says otherwise: with Speed 2, an Action that lets you Evade 3 lets you Evade only 2. Forced Movement and Reposition don't use your Speed.

No movement ends in another creature's square: an Advance, an Evade, a Forced Movement or a Reposition (passing through one is covered under Move and Difficult Terrain).

Changes to your Speed. Apply every other change first, then halve it: with Speed 6, Weight of Judgment's −2 and Hindered, your Speed is (6 − 2) halved = 2. Halving rounds down.

Advance

Advance is the normal movement, and the Action every creature uses to move. You only move with an Action that moves you: Advance, Evade, or another Action that says so (someone else moving you, with Forced Movement or Reposition, is not you moving). An Advance can trigger reactions.

An Advance is one piece. You move once, up to the distance, and stop: the movement you don't use is lost. You can't move part of an Advance, use another Action, then move the rest later. For instance, with Speed 5 you can't Advance 2, make a Weapon Attack and then Advance the other 3: that is two Advance Actions.

Interact during an Advance. During the Advance Action, at any one point of the movement, you can use the Interact Action (draw a weapon, open a door on the way, help an ally stand up), paying its 1 AP then, and go on with the same Advance. Once an Advance, and only in the Advance Action used on its own: not in an Advance that is part of another Action (a Linked Action such as "Advance 5, make a Weapon Attack (1A) and Advance 5 again", a Setup such as "Setup: Advance 3", or a Charge), unless its card says so, and not during an Evade.

A Reaction that triggers on your movement can fire only once for an Advance, at the square the reacting creature chooses (see Reactions).

Evade

Evade is a type of movement that doesn't trigger reactions. You can't Evade into or pass through Difficult Terrain. What an Evade costs is decided by the Action that lets you Evade, such as the Evade Action. The Evade Action doesn't have the Move trait.

An Evade is one piece too, and nothing fits inside it: if an Action lets you Evade 3 and you Evade 1 square, the other 2 squares are lost.

When an Action allows you to Evade, you can use the movement as an Advance instead. By itself this brings no benefit, but it lets a creature move willingly through reactions, or through Difficult Terrain, where an Evade can't go. A creature that can't use Move Actions (Immobilized) or is Prone can't use the movement as an Advance either.

Flying

To be decided

Flying isn't written yet: going up and down, ending a turn in the air, falling when knocked Prone or Immobilized. Until it is, a creature that flies hovers just above the ground: it moves as on the ground, and the GM rules where flying matters.

Moving and Leaving Your Square

Rules ask three different questions about movement, and the answers are not the same:

Movement A Move Action You moved You left your square
Advance, Charge, Crawl Yes Yes Yes
Evade No Yes Yes
Stand Yes No No
Forced Movement (Pushed, Pulled and Slid) No No Yes
Reposition No No Yes
  • Move with a capital letter always means a Move Action: an Action with the Move trait. "Until you use a Move Action" ends only with a Move Action.
  • "You haven't moved" is about your own movement: moving with an Action, Evade included. Forced Movement and Reposition are not you moving, and standing up is not moving.
  • "You haven't left your square" is about any change of position, Forced Movement and Reposition included. A creature that occupies several squares leaves its square when any square it occupies changes.

Corners

You can't cut solid corners when you move. Moving diagonally takes you through the corner point where four squares meet. If a wall or anything solid occupies that point, the corner is solid and you can't move diagonally past it: you must go around. A wall that ends exactly at the corner counts, and so does a pillar that stands on the corner or an object that fills a square beside your path, because each of them reaches the point. A small object in the middle of a square doesn't reach the corner, so it doesn't block the diagonal. This applies to every movement of yours (Advance, Evade, Charge) and to Forced Movement and Reposition. A creature that occupies several squares follows the rule with each square it occupies.

Creatures aren't solid corners: you can move diagonally between two creatures. If both are unwilling, this is Difficult Terrain, as if you were passing through the squares of an unwilling creature; a willing creature lets you pass. If a Forced Movement would move a creature diagonally between two creatures, it doesn't pass through them: it stops in the last legal square and Collision applies as normal. A Reposition can't pass between two creatures either: it stops in the last legal square, without Collision damage.

You (Y) move diagonally. A red X is a solid corner: you must go around. A green dot is an open corner.

Straight Line

When an Action, effect or rule moves a creature (yourself included) in a straight line, like the Charge Action, draw a line from the center of the creature's square to the center of the destination square. The creature moves along the same squares as a Line: one square per step along the line's longer direction, at each step the square whose center is nearest to the line, ending in the destination. Where the line passes exactly between two squares, choose a side once, left or right (looking toward the destination), for the whole movement: every tie takes that side. The creature that moves chooses for its own movement; the origin chooses for a Forced Movement. If a square on the line isn't a legal move (for Charge: Difficult Terrain, a creature in the way, or a solid corner), the movement stops in the last legal square before it.

Toward a creature. When a rule moves you in a straight line toward a creature, the line goes to the center of that creature's space. You can stop in any square on the line, and you can't enter the creature's space: the movement brings you closer to it, never around it.

In the figures, Y is you. Blue squares are the squares the token passes, the green square is where it ends, and red squares are not legal. The line is what counts: the path of the token on the grid does not have to be exactly straight, because a token moves from square to square.

Forced Movement

Forced Movement is movement you impose on another creature, choosing where it goes. There are three types: Pushed, Pulled and Slid. Reposition also moves a creature of your choice, but it isn't Forced Movement. Every Forced Movement follows these rules:

  • It doesn't trigger Reactions from movement. (A Reaction that triggers on the Forced Movement itself, "a creature would be moved by Forced Movement", still does.)
  • It ignores Difficult Terrain.
  • It can move a creature into Hazardous Terrain or a Deadly Hazard.
  • It doesn't use the creature's Speed, and each square counts as 1, even when it is diagonal.
  • Its value is reduced by the creature's Steadiness.
  • The origin of Forced Movement is the creature using the Action, unless the effect names another creature or a point as its origin ("Pushed 1, away from the target", "Pushed 2 from the Burst's center"): the direction is then taken from there, and the creature using the Action still chooses the destinations.
  • Its value is a maximum: you can always move the creature less, down to 0. Moving a creature 0 squares is no movement and no Forced Movement on it: nothing that happens when a creature is moved, enters or leaves a square happens. It can never make a creature end its movement inside another creature or an object: this is Collision, and it only happens when the destination you chose is blocked.

Pushed

Being Pushed is a Forced Movement. Pushed has a value: up to that many squares you are moved. The origin chooses the destination. Each square you are pushed into must be farther from the origin than the previous one (measured in a straight line between the centers of the squares), and the path must stay within a cone spreading from the origin through you.

That cone is every step going in a direction within 45° of the straight line from the origin to you. Each square counts as 1 toward the value, even when it is diagonal. The 45° edge counts for Pushed. It doesn't for Pulled, whose cone is narrower.

If something blocks the way to the destination the origin chose, Collision applies.

Example

A goblin stands directly below you and you use Pushed 3 on them. They can end in any square in the cone shown below: 1 square to the side after 1 step, 2 after 2 steps, and 3 after 3 steps. They can't be moved sideways or back toward you. If the goblin were diagonal from you, the cone would point diagonally.

The numbered squares are where G can end, and the number is how many steps it takes.

Pulled

Being Pulled is a Forced Movement, the opposite of Pushed. Pulled has a value: up to that many squares you are moved. The origin chooses the destination. Each square you are pulled into must be closer to the origin than the previous one (measured in a straight line between the centers of the squares), and the path must stay inside a cone that has its apex on you and points toward the origin.

That cone is every direction less than 45° from the straight line from you to the origin: the 45° edge is not part of it. Each square counts as 1 toward the value, even when it is diagonal. A creature that is next to the origin can't be pulled any closer, so it stops there.

You can't be pulled into the origin's square. The origin can end the movement next to it, or choose its own square as the destination: then Collision applies, with the origin as the creature in the way, and both take damage for the unused squares.

Example

A goblin stands directly above you, 3 squares away, and you use Pulled 3 on them. They can end in any square in the cone shown below: straight toward you after 1 step, or any of the 3 squares next to you after 2 steps. Then they stop. You can leave them there, with no damage, or choose your own square as the destination: the 3rd square is then unused, Collision applies and you and the goblin take 1 damage each.

The numbered squares are where G can end, and the number is how many steps it takes. You can stop G next to you, or name your own square as the destination: G stops next to you and Collision applies.

Slid

Being Slid is a Forced Movement. Slid has a value: up to that many squares of path you are moved. The origin chooses the destination and the exact path the creature takes: a Slid can curve, moving the creature closer to the origin, farther from it, or sideways.

Each square of the path must be next to the previous one, and each counts as 1 toward the value, even when it is diagonal. The path can't cross a wall or pass through an object, and it can't pass through another creature's square or the origin's: if the path the origin chose does, Collision applies at that point. The origin must have Line of Effect to the creature at every square of the path; if it would lose it, the movement ends there (that is not a Collision, so there is no damage).

Example

A goblin stands 2 squares east of you, with a brazier (Hazardous Terrain) in the square between you. You use Slid 3: the goblin goes 1 square northwest, then 1 west, ending in the square directly north of you. It used 2 of its 3 squares, passed beside the brazier without entering it, and you had Line of Effect to it all along. The path curved: the value counted squares of path, not straight-line distance.

The numbered squares are the path, in order. The thin green lines are the Line of Effect from you (Y): it must reach G at every square.

Collision

Collision happens when something is in the way of the destination the origin chose. For Pushed and Pulled, calculate it from the center of the creature: draw a line from where the creature started to where the Forced Movement was meant to end. For Slid, follow the path the origin chose. If something is in the way, the creature stops in the last legal square the line or the path passes through: a square where the whole creature fits and that has no object or creature in it.

A creature that stops short takes Lethal Blunt Vigor damage for its unused squares: the squares between where it stopped and the destination the origin chose.

  • An object (a wall, a closed door, etc.): 2 damage for each unused square.
  • Another creature, or the origin: 1 damage for each unused square, to each of the two creatures.

The origin decides how far to aim. If it chooses a destination the creature can reach, there is no Collision and no damage: moving a creature less than the value never hurts it.

Example

Pushed 4 aimed at a destination 4 squares away, with a wall right behind you, deals 8 damage. Aimed through a creature after 1 square, it deals 3 damage to each. Pushed 1 square, with nothing in the way, deals no damage.

A Reposition stops at an object or a creature without taking Collision damage.

Reposition

Reposition moves a creature of your choice along a path, but it isn't Forced Movement. Reposition has a value: up to that many squares of path. Your Reach and the creature's Size don't limit it. The path follows the rules of Slid (each square next to the previous one, each counting as 1 even when it is diagonal, and the origin must have Line of Effect to the creature at every square), with these rules:

  • It doesn't trigger Reactions from movement.
  • It ignores Difficult Terrain.
  • Its value is reduced by the creature's Steadiness.
  • It can't move a creature into Hazardous Terrain or a Deadly Hazard, though it can move the creature to a less advantageous position, for example into a flanked square.
  • It can't pass through creatures or objects: it stops in the last legal square before one, without Collision damage. It can never make a creature end its movement inside another creature or an object.
Example

Dave stands between you and a goblin, in a line, with an empty square between you and Dave. Reposition 2 can't move the goblin through Dave's square, but the path can go around him: 1 square diagonally over Dave, then 1 square diagonally down, into the empty square next to you.

The numbered squares are the path, in order. The red line is the straight way through Dave: a Reposition can't pass through a creature.

The four movements side by side:

Pushed Pulled Slid Reposition
Forced Movement Yes Yes Yes No
Direction Away (cone) Toward (cone) Any path Any path
The origin needs Line of Effect at every square of the path No No Yes Yes
Into Hazardous Terrain or a Deadly Hazard Yes Yes Yes No
Creatures in the way Collision Collision Collision Stops, no damage
Objects in the way Collision damage Collision damage Collision damage Stops, no damage
Each diagonal square counts 1 1 1 1

All four need Line of Effect to the creature when they begin, like anything a card does to a creature (see Targets of Effects); the table's row is about the rest of the path.

Swapping Places

When a rule makes two creatures swap squares, each enters the square the other left, at the same moment. Each of them is moved by a Reposition: it is not a Move Action, it triggers no Reactions, and both have left their square (see Moving and Leaving Your Square).

Only two creatures of the same Size can swap squares. Steadiness doesn't stop a swap with a willing creature: it chooses not to apply it.

Steadiness

Some creatures are harder to move than others. Every creature has a Steadiness: normally 0, and never negative. When you are moved by Forced Movement or Reposition, reduce its value by your Steadiness: a Pushed 3 against Steadiness 1 is a Pushed 2, and a value of 0 or less moves you nowhere.
