The value is reduced before the origin chooses the destination, so a creature with Steadiness also takes less damage from Collision (the origin can aim less far). You can choose not to apply your Steadiness, for example when an ally helps you.

Difficult Terrain

Each square of difficult terrain counts double the squares it would normally count. The GM decides where it is (rubble, deep snow...). Darkness is Difficult Terrain for creatures that can't see in it. Passing through the squares of an unwilling creature is Difficult Terrain too.

Hazardous Terrain

Hazardous Terrain is any terrain that deals damage or inflicts a harmful condition on the creatures in it. The effect that creates it is marked [HT] in its text and declares one or more trigger patterns.

[HT] is notation, like [W] and [Mod]: it is written in the text of the effect that creates the area, not among the Action's traits (a Weapon Attack whose Tier 2 leaves caltrops is not a hazard itself). It declares its pattern(s) after a colon, such as [HT: Entering] or [HT: Entering, Turn]: "The area lasts 2 rounds [HT: Entering, Turn]." The three patterns are:

  • Entering: "When a creature enters this area." A creature in the area when it appears is treated as entering it.
  • Turn: "When a creature ends its turn in this area."
  • Movement: "When a creature moves within this area." A movement (an Advance, an Evade or a Forced Movement) that crosses any square of the area.

An [HT] effect with no declared pattern uses Entering and Turn by default.

Once per turn-cycle. An [HT] area affects each creature at most once per turn-cycle (from the start of that creature's turn to the start of its next), whatever its patterns: a creature that Advances into an area with Entering and Movement, or enters it and ends its turn there, is affected once.

Size. An [HT] area affects a creature once regardless of its Size.

Example

A 2 Emanation of fire (Distance 10 sq.) has [HT: Entering, Turn]. A creature that walks into it takes [V] 1d8 Fi damage on entering; a creature already inside takes the same damage when it ends its turn there. A creature that enters, leaves and re-enters with a different Movement in the same turn-cycle is affected at most once.

Deadly Hazards

Some hazards kill at once: a fall into a chasm, a pit of lava, a crushing trap. These are Deadly Hazards. A Forced Movement into one kills Minor enemies, and a Reposition can't move a creature into a Deadly Hazard at all (see Reposition). Any other creature, Player Characters included, isn't killed: they barely avoid it and are Imperiled, for example hanging from the edge of the chasm.

A creature that enters a Deadly Hazard voluntarily (by its own movement, or by choosing not to escape) also chooses: it is either Imperiled or outright killed.

Reach

Reach is how far your body reaches: how far you can interact with things in the world. By default, every Species has a Reach of 1: you can reach 1 square from your position.

When an Action shows "Reach" as its distance (touching an ally, grabbing an object, tripping a creature), it means your Reach. Weapons don't change your Reach: they have a Range of their own (see Weapon Range, where a Reach above 1 adds to the Range of your melee weapons).

You can't target a creature or an object beyond the distance of an Action (its Reach or its range).

The numbers are the distance in squares from the creature in the middle.

Weapon Range

Every weapon has a Range, melee weapons included. An Action whose distance is Weapon uses the Range of the weapon you use for it. Weapon Actions have that distance unless they say otherwise.

  • How it is written. A Range is written like the ranges of ranged weapons: normal / far (1 Bane) / maximum (2 Banes). A single number is a normal range with no far or maximum range. Most melee weapons have Range 1; a lance has Range 1 / 2.
  • Reach above 1. Your Reach above 1 adds to every number of the Range of your melee weapons: with Reach 2, a lance attacks at 2 / 3. It doesn't change the Range of a ranged or thrown attack.
  • Long. A weapon with the Long property takes 1 Field Bane against adjacent creatures. A pike with Range 3 and Long is at its best 2 or 3 squares away.

Weapon Actions and Your Weapon

A Weapon Action takes its distance and its Melee or Ranged nature from the weapon you use for it, and from how you use it. With a Ranged weapon, or a weapon with the Thrown property when thrown, it uses the weapon's ranged Range and counts as a Ranged Action (Prone's Bane applies to it). With a Melee weapon used in hand, it uses the weapon's melee Range and counts as a Melee Action (Prone's Boon applies). An Action that has the Melee or Ranged trait itself needs a weapon used that way. While you have a free hand, you can use your Fists as your weapon.

Engaged

You are Engaged if you are adjacent to an enemy (next to you, even diagonally) and both of you can be Engaged. Being Engaged does not depend on what you perceive: an enemy next to you that you cannot see still Engages you.

A condition can say that you can't be Engaged, as Unconscious does. A creature that can't be Engaged is never Engaged, and the creatures next to it are not Engaged with it.

By itself, being Engaged does nothing. Other rules use the word, such as Ranged Combat While Engaged below.

Ranged Combat While Engaged

Using a [Ranged] Action while you are Engaged is very hard: the roll is Doomed.

When you use a [Ranged] Action against a creature that is Engaged with a creature other than yourself, you suffer 1 Field Bane.

Flanking

A creature threatens every enemy within the normal range of a Melee weapon, for as long as it qualifies to use that weapon's Weapon Attack (1A). The 3-Strike limit doesn't remove the threat: it prevents using the Action, not qualifying for it. Some conditions, such as Unconscious, cause a creature to threaten no one, and a weapon with the Non-threatening property doesn't threaten, unless a feature says otherwise. The far range of a Melee weapon doesn't count, and a Melee weapon with the Long property doesn't threaten adjacent enemies.

Like Engaged, threatening does not depend on what you perceive, but it uses range and not adjacency: a creature with a Range 2 weapon threatens an enemy 2 squares away, which is not Engaged with it.

Creatures that threaten the same enemy flank it. A creature that flanks an enemy gains 1 Field Boon on its [Melee] Actions against that enemy for each other creature that flanks it. But each ally of that enemy that threatens the flanker cancels 1 of those Boons, and a creature never gains fewer than 0. Count in this order: 1 for each other flanker, minus 1 for each ally of the enemy that threatens you (never below 0); only then does the limit of 2 Field Boons apply (see Named Boons and Banes).

Blue tokens are allies and red-brown tokens are enemies. A badge is the Boons that creature gets on [Melee] Actions against the creature in the middle (G, John in the fifth picture) or against D in the last one.

Example 1: Two flankers. Philip and John both threaten a goblin: each has 1 Boon on [Melee] Actions against it.

Example 2: Three flankers. A third ally threatens it too: 2 Field Boons each, which is the limit.

Example 3: Four or more. A fourth ally adds no Boon, but it still counts for cancelling: if an ally of the goblin threatens one of the flankers, that flanker keeps 2 (3 minus 1, then the limit).

Example 4: Range 2. Philip holds a weapon with Range 2 and stands 2 squares from the goblin. He threatens it, so he flanks with John, who is next to it: 1 Boon each.

Example 5: Three goblins on John. Three goblins threaten John, and Philip stands next to two of them. The goblin on the left has the other two goblins flanking with it and no ally of John's next to it: 2 Boons. The other two also have 2 goblins flanking with them, but Philip threatens each of them and cancels 1: 1 Boon each.

Example 6: Two lines of fighters. Two lines of fighters face each other, all of them against D, the second fighter on the left. Each fighter has allies beside it that threaten the enemies in front of them, so almost every Boon is cancelled: D's neighbors cancel the Boons, and only a fighter at the very end of a line can still gain 1, against the second fighter of the other line.

Line of Effect

To target a creature with an Action, or to do anything to a creature with a card or a feature (see Targets of Effects), you need Line of Effect to them: a straight line from the center of your square to any corner of the target's space that nothing blocks. Walls and similar solid obstacles block a line. If all four corners are blocked, you have no Line of Effect and can't target the creature, even if you perceive it.

An area effect checks Line of Effect from its Point of Origin to each creature in the area (from the center of the space, when the Point of Origin is a creature's space).

A Large creature (2x2 squares or bigger) uses the four corners of its whole space. A Large creature that is the one targeting picks any square it occupies as its starting square.

A line that only touches the end of a wall isn't blocked.

To be decided

Targeting walls and objects (and the Breach trait, to hit a creature behind a wall you break) is not written yet.

Cover

Cover is how well a target is protected from you. Count the corners of the target's space that are blocked from the center of your square:

Blocked corners Cover Effect on your Actions against it
0 None None
1 Low 1 Field Bane
2 Medium 2 Field Banes
3 High Doomed (and no Field Banes from the Cover)
4 Total No Line of Effect: you can't target them
  • Creatures in the way. If another creature is on the line from the center of your square to the center of the target's space, the target has Low cover (1 Field Bane). Against an area, the creatures inside it never give cover (Cover against an area). Creatures never count as blocked corners, and cover doesn't add up: you take the highest cover that applies.
  • Cover and the rest. Cover applies to melee and ranged Actions alike. Its Field Banes count with your other Field Banes. High cover gives no Field Banes, only Doomed; your other Field Banes still apply (Prone, Obscured). A target that is Hidden and behind High cover is still only Doomed once.

The same attacker (A) and wall in the first five panels; only the target (T) moves. Green lines reach a corner of the target's space; red lines are blocked (X). In the last panel a creature (X) is on the line between the centers: Low cover.

Leaning

A creature behind a wall can lean out to attack. While you are Leaning, you calculate cover from one of your corners instead of the center of your square, and your own cover against other creatures' Actions is reduced by 1 level (Total → High → Medium → Low → none). A creature leaning out of Total cover becomes High cover (still targetable). Leaning lasts until the end of your turn, so Reactions can use it. You can stop Leaning at any time on your turn, at no cost. See the Leaning Basic Action.

Areas

Some Actions have an Area, written on its own line, for example Area: 1 Emanation. These Actions have the Area trait. An Area Action can also have a Distance, on the next line: how far from the creature using the Action its area can be placed, for example Distance: 10 sq. With no Distance, an Emanation is around the creature that uses the Action.

Every area spreads from a Point of Origin: for an Emanation, its target (a creature's space or a square); for a Line, your square; for other areas, the point the Action says they start from (for example, the tip of a cone). The Point of Origin is a place, not the creature that uses the Action, which is still called the origin.

Cover against an area

Line of Effect and Cover are checked from the area's Point of Origin to each creature in it. The creatures inside an area never give Cover against it, to each other or to themselves: only walls and objects do. For example, an Ogre slams the ground in a 2 Emanation around itself with three Goblins and Wes in it: Wes, behind a Goblin, gets no Cover from that Goblin, but a pillar between the Ogre and Wes still gives him Cover.

Emanation

An Emanation, written with a value like 1 Emanation, extends a number of squares around its target: a creature or a square. It affects every creature in its area unless the Action says otherwise. If its target is a creature, the origin decides whether that creature is affected too. For example, a creature using Ground Slam (an Emanation around itself) decides whether it is affected.

An Emanation around a creature extends that many squares from every square the creature occupies, so it follows the creature's Size. A 1 Emanation around a Medium (3) creature covers 3 × 3 squares (its square and the 8 around it); around a Huge (5) creature, which occupies 3 × 3, it covers 5 × 5. A Distance of 10 sq. means the Emanation is placed up to 10 squares from the creature using the Action; with no Distance, it is around that creature.

Aura

An Aura is an area that follows its origin. It extends a number of squares from every square the origin occupies (the same footprint as an Emanation around that creature) and moves with them. It is written with a value, like Aura 2, and its Point of Origin is always the creature it belongs to. The origin decides whether they are affected themselves. A creature gains an Aura's effect as soon as it enters the Aura, and loses it when it leaves. An Emanation, by contrast, is placed at a target and stays there.

Burst

A Burst, written with a value like 2 Burst, is centered on a corner, the point where four squares meet, never on the center of a square or on a creature. It affects every square whose center is within that many squares of the corner, measured in a straight line: a 1 Burst covers the 4 squares around the corner, and a 2 Burst covers 12 (a 4 × 4 block without its corners). Otherwise it works like an Emanation: it affects every creature in its area unless the Action says otherwise, and its Point of Origin is the corner, placed within the Action's Distance.

The dot is the corner the Burst is centered on.

Line

A Line, written with a value like Line 10, is a row of squares that always starts from you: its Point of Origin is the center of your square, as for an Aura. It has no Distance: its value is how far it reaches.

Aim it at any square. Draw a segment from the center of your square through the center of that square, and take one square per step along the segment's longer direction: at each step, the square whose center is nearest to the segment. The first square is the one next to you. The Line goes on past the square you aimed at until the next square would be farther from you than its value (counted like any distance: every second diagonal counts 2). Only those squares are the Line, never every square the segment touches. A Line 10 is 10 squares straight, 8 squares at a slope like 2 to 1 or 5 to 2, and 7 squares on a diagonal.

  • Ties. Where the segment passes exactly between two squares, choose a side before rolling: left or right, seen from above looking from you toward the square you aimed at. Every tie in that Line takes that side. A Line with no ties has nothing to choose. Both sides give the same number of squares, though not always the same shape.
  • Larger creatures. A creature bigger than Medium starts the Line from one of the squares of its space on the side it aims toward.
  • Walls. A Line stops at the first square it can't enter (a wall or a solid obstacle): the squares behind it are not part of the Line. This matters for a Line that stays on the map, or Hazardous Terrain.
  • Height. A Line is 1 square high unless the Action says otherwise: it doesn't reach a creature flying above its squares.
  • Targets and cover. A Line affects every creature in its squares unless the Action says otherwise, and the Action is rolled once for all of them. Line of Effect and Cover are checked from your square, as for any area, and the creatures in the Line give no cover to each other (walls still do; see Cover against an area).
  • No range Banes. The Line's value is its reach, so a weapon's far or maximum range adds no Banes inside it. Other Banes still apply: Engaged for a [Ranged] Action, Cover from walls.
Example

You use a Line 6 and aim at the square 2 squares east and 1 south of you. The segment passes exactly between two squares at the first, third and fifth steps. You choose left: the Line takes the square directly east of you, then goes 1 south for every 2 squares east, 5 squares in all (the 6th would be 7 squares away). Had you chosen right, it would start with the square diagonally southeast of you: a different shape, the same 5 squares.

Y is you. The number in each square is its distance from you, counted as for any distance. The dashed line is the segment from the center of your square through the square you aim at (outlined).

Orange squares are ties (the segment passes exactly between two squares): every tie takes the side you chose. Dashed squares are the other side, not taken.

Y is you. The dashed line is the segment; the outlined square is the one aimed at.

Other areas

Other areas (cones) also affect every creature in them unless the Action says otherwise. Line of Effect and Cover are checked from the Point of Origin to each creature, and the Action is rolled once for all its targets.

To be decided

Cones are not written yet (and Lines wider than 1 square).

Light

Light affects Sight (see Senses): the light where a creature is decides how well you see it.

A light source sheds Bright light in an Emanation of its size, and Dim light for the same number of squares beyond that. A torch with Bright light 4 gives Bright light in a 4 Emanation and Dim light from 5 to 8 squares away (an 8 Emanation). Lantern of Faith's Bright light 3 gives Bright light in a 3 Emanation and Dim light from 4 to 6. Beyond that, the light of the scene applies (daylight, night, a dark cave...).

A light has the same shape as an area: around a creature or an object it is an Emanation, counted from every square it occupies, and a light placed on a corner is a Burst. So a Bright light 2 reaches the same squares as a 2 Emanation, and its Dim light works the same way with its own size.

Bright squares: strong color. Dim squares: pale. The torch is the dot in the middle.

Light never makes a square darker: where several lights reach, use the brightest one. A torch carried in daylight changes nothing. A creature is in one light level at a time, so its penalties never stack. A creature bigger than one square is in the brightest light of any square it occupies: you see the part of it that is lit.

Bright

You see creatures in Bright light Clearly, and you move normally. Bright light is daylight outside, or the Bright light of a light source.

Dim

When you target something that is in Dim light, the target is Obscured (see Senses). Dim light is twilight, a full moon, or the Dim light of a light source, such as the edge of a bonfire's light.

Darkness

When you target something that is in Darkness, you can't see it: it is Hidden if you perceive it some other way, and Unsensed if you don't (see Senses). Squares in darkness are Difficult Terrain for you.

Senses

You perceive creatures through your senses. Each sense lets you perceive some creatures as Clear, Obscured or Hidden. Use your best sense for each creature; a sense never makes a creature harder to perceive. A creature you perceive with none of your senses is Unsensed.

Perception Your Actions against it Its Actions against you
Clear Normal. Normal.
Obscured 1 Field Bane. 1 Field Boon, if it is Clear to you.
Hidden Doomed. Favored.
Unsensed You can't target it. Favored.

Actions with the Area trait ignore Senses: they target the creatures in their area however well you perceive them.

When you use an Action against a creature, ask two questions, in this order:

  1. How do you perceive it? That is the "Your Actions against it" column: nothing if it is Clear, 1 Field Bane if it is Obscured, Doomed if it is Hidden. If it is Unsensed, you can't target it.
  2. Does it perceive you worse than you perceive it? Only then do you gain the "Its Actions against you" column, read for how it perceives you: 1 Field Boon if you are Obscured to it, Favored if you are Hidden or Unsensed to it. You never gain this against a creature that is Hidden to you.

Y is you; G is a goblin. Both have only Sight and Hearing. Yellow square: Bright light; pale: Dim light; dark: Darkness. A curved dashed arrow is how one perceives the other; a straight arrow is what that gives its Actions. Green is good for the one acting, orange is bad.

So two creatures that are each Obscured to the other each take 1 Field Bane and gain nothing, and two creatures that are each Hidden to the other are both Doomed against each other. A roll that is both Favored and Doomed is a normal roll (see Favored and Doomed Rolls).

Every creature has Sight and Hearing:

  • Sight: You perceive creatures in Bright light as Clear and creatures in Dim light as Obscured. You can't see creatures in Darkness, or creatures you have no Line of Effect to.
  • Hearing: You perceive creatures that make noise within 10 squares as Hidden, even through walls. Creatures in combat make noise, even standing in the same square on their turn. A creature can Hide to stop making noise.

So in Darkness you usually still hear a creature, and it is Hidden to you; an invisible creature that you only hear is Hidden too.

To be decided

Hiding and sneaking are not written yet.

Sight Senses

Sight Senses change how light works for your Sight. They also remove the Difficult Terrain of Darkness.

  • Dim-light Sight: For your Sight, Dim light counts as Bright.
  • Dark Sight: For your Sight, Dim light and Darkness count as Bright.

Other Senses

Other senses work in any light, but only within their range and conditions, and only to perceive creatures: they don't help your Rolls that require sight. Some examples:

  • Lesser Heatsight (6 sq.): You perceive creatures within 6 squares as Obscured, if they give off heat or are much colder than their surroundings.
  • Heatsight (6 sq.): As Lesser Heatsight, but you perceive them as Clear.
  • Tremorsense (6 sq.): You perceive creatures within 6 squares as Clear, if they touch the same ground as you and no thick wall is between you.
Example

A Goblin with Dark Sight stands in Darkness, and Krysta, who has only Sight and Hearing, stands in Bright torchlight. Krysta can only hear the Goblin, so it is Hidden to her: her Actions against it are Doomed, and its Actions against her are Favored. The Goblin sees Krysta Clearly.

A Snake with Lesser Heatsight attacks Krysta in the same Darkness. Krysta is warm, so the Snake perceives her as Obscured (1 Bane on its Actions), while she only hears the Snake (Hidden: Doomed against it, and the Snake is Favored against her). In Dim light, the Snake's heatsight would give it nothing more than its Sight.

A Cave Worm with Tremorsense loses Krysta when she climbs a rope. If she is also quiet (she Hides) and it is dark, she is Unsensed: the Worm can't target her.

Krysta and a Goblin, neither with Dark Sight, fight in Darkness. Each only hears the other, so each is Hidden to the other: both are Doomed against each other, and neither is Favored.

The GM decides how each creature perceives each other when it isn't obvious.

Chapter 4: Health

Health Pool

Your Health Pool is the sum of two thresholds, Vigor and Resolve:

  1. Your class gives a high and a low Health value. When you build your character, you assign one to Vigor and the other to Resolve; the choice can't be changed later.
  2. Your species adds its bonus to each (see the Species document).
  3. Your Stage: at Stages 1, 2 and 3, each threshold grows by your class's step for its value (the high step or the low step; see Stages).
  4. The floor: neither threshold can be less than a third of your Health Pool (rounded up). If one is, move points from the other threshold to it until it reaches a third; the Health Pool doesn't change.

Your Attributes don't change your Health.

Example

A Human Paladin (high 20, low 10) puts the high value on Vigor: Vigor 20 + 3 = 23, Resolve 10 + 2 = 12, Health Pool 35.

Steven, an Elf Archer (high 16, low 8), puts the high value on Resolve: Vigor 8 + 1 = 9, Resolve 16 + 4 = 20, Health Pool 29. A third of 29 is 10, so 1 point moves: Vigor 10, Resolve 19.

Vigor and Resolve are not separate pools. All damage reduces the same Health Pool. The thresholds only decide which states you reach.

Damage

Record every point of damage as:

  • Vigor or Resolve (see Damage Types)
  • Lethal or Nonlethal

Damage is Lethal unless an Action or effect says it is Nonlethal. Lethal and Nonlethal damage both count toward the thresholds and toward your total damage. They never cancel or convert each other. Damage keeps accumulating after you are Down.

When you have Vigor damage equal to or more than your Vigor, you are Bloodied. When you have Resolve damage equal to or more than your Resolve, you are Strained.

Instances of Damage

An Action's damage can come in several instances: each part with its own pool and damage type is one instance. "[V] 1[W] + [Mod] + [R] 2d8 Ho" deals two: the weapon's damage with your Modifier (Vigor, the weapon's type), and 2d8 Holy (Resolve). Each [W] is its own instance (2[W] is two, see the Gear document), and extra damage from another effect is its own instance. Each target takes its own instances. Rules that count instances count them this way.

Lethal and Nonlethal

Actions deal Lethal damage by default. Actions with the Nonlethal trait deal Nonlethal damage by default. A Nonlethal Action can deal Lethal damage by taking a Bane, and a Lethal Action can deal Nonlethal damage by taking a Bane as well. A Save Action doesn't roll, so it switches the other way: every creature that makes its Save gains 1 Boon on it.

How damage is written on a card ([V], [R], [W], [Mod] and the damage types) is in Roll Effects. Empowered, which adds a die to your damage, is in Conditions.

Going Down

When your total damage equals or goes above your Health Pool, you are Down. Follow these steps in order:

  1. Nonlethal damage ≥ 50% of your Health Pool: you fall Unconscious.
  2. Some Nonlethal damage, but under 50%, and the damage that took you Down was Nonlethal: choose to fall Unconscious or keep fighting as Desperate.
  3. Otherwise (no Nonlethal damage, or a Lethal blow took you Down): check your Dominant Damage and become Dying or Shattered.

Getting Back Up

When your damage drops below your Health Pool, you are no longer Down: Desperate, Dying and Shattered end, and if you are Unconscious, you wake up at once.

NPCs Going Down

When an NPC goes Down, they die if they have more Lethal damage, or fall Unconscious if they have more Nonlethal damage. If they are equal, the GM chooses.

Dominant Damage

Compare your total Vigor damage to your total Resolve damage. The higher one is your Dominant Damage. On a tie, the creature that goes Down chooses.

Dominant Damage doesn't do anything by itself, but it determines the condition you gain when you go Down. Some abilities might also make use of it. You know which Dominant Damage a creature has if you perceive them (Hidden is enough).

  • Vigor is dominant: you become Dying.
  • Resolve is dominant: you become Shattered.

Wounds and the Tables

Every result on the Dying or Shattered Table is a Wound. A Wound from the Dying Table is a Body Wound. A Wound from the Shattered Table is a Mind Wound.

Roll: 2d12 (no exploding dice) − your Body (Dying) or Mind (Shattered) + 1d6 per Wound of the same kind you already have (Body Wounds for the Dying Table, Mind Wounds for the Shattered Table).

Example: a character with 3 Body and 1 Body Wound rolls 2d12 − 3 + 1d6 on the Dying Table.

Result Outcome
4 or less Something very minor
5 to 8 Something minor
9 to 12 Something minor
13 to 16 Something moderate
17 to 20 Something moderate
21 to 23 Something severe
24 Something severe
25 to 26 "Soft" death
27 or more Death
To be decided

The entries of the Dying and Shattered Tables are placeholders.

Rally Points

Each character begins with Rally Points equal to your class's Rally value + 1, and 1 more at each Stage after Stage 0 (Rally + 2 at Stage 1, + 3 at Stage 2, + 4 at Stage 3).

When a Rally Point is used, normally with Steel Yourself, the target removes ⌈their Health Pool ÷ 4⌉ damage. You choose which damage to remove.

Heal. When a feature says a creature heals a number, it removes that much damage. The creature chooses which damage, as with a Rally Point. A heal to several creatures is rolled once: each of them heals that much.

If you are Exhausted, use your Health Pool as if you weren't: Exhausted doesn't lower your Rally Points or the damage each one removes.

While Down (Desperate, Dying or Shattered) or Unconscious, you can't use Steel Yourself. Other Actions can still let you use Rally Points, such as Lay On Hands.

Nonlethal damage is removed like any other damage.

Only a Rest restores Rally Points. Sleep does not. A new encounter does not.

NPCs. NPCs have no Rally Points. When an Action lets an NPC use one (an ally's Lay On Hands on it) or measures something in its Rally Points (Guard equal to what one of their Rally Points heals), one of its Rally Points removes 9 damage at Stage 0, and it spends nothing (the later Stages' numbers come with their Bestiary tables).

Guard

Some effects give you Guard, written with a value: Guard 6. When you take damage, your Guard takes it first (Vigor or Resolve damage alike), and only the rest reaches your Health. Damage your Guard takes isn't damage you take: it doesn't count toward your thresholds or your Health Pool, and it doesn't trigger anything that happens when you take damage. A rider on that damage still happens: a rider happens whatever damage is dealt.

  • Damage reduction (such as Shield of Faith) applies first; Guard takes what is left. Reductions from different effects add up (Judge's and Shield of Faith's), and each applies once to an Action's damage to that creature, after Resist.
  • Guard isn't Health: it can't be healed, and Rally Points don't restore it.
  • It doesn't stack: if you gain Guard while you have some, keep the higher value (see Stacking). The exception is the Guard your Unspent AP give you: it adds to your other Guard, damage takes it first, and it lasts 1 round (from the start of your turn until you regain AP again).
  • It ends at the end of the encounter.
Example

Zack has Guard 6 and takes 8 Vigor damage: his Guard takes 6 and ends, and he takes 2 Vigor damage.

Recovery

There are three ways to recover, from shortest to longest: a Breather, a Sleep and a Rest.

Take a Breather

Taking a Breather is 10 minutes of rest. It removes all of your Nonlethal damage. It is not a Rest (see below).

Sleep

Sleep is 8 hours of non-strenuous activity, such as sleeping or keeping a quiet watch. You can complete a Sleep at most once every 16 hours. Completing a Sleep lets you use your Daily Actions again.

If you go 24 hours without completing a Sleep, you are Exhausted 1. The value increases by 1 for every further 24 hours without one.

Completing a Sleep reduces your Exhausted value by 2.

Rest

To complete a Rest, a character spends a day (24 hours) resting in a safe place. A Rest includes a Sleep.

A safe place is a place where you are sure you can rest safely, such as a town. The GM decides what is a safe place. Towns are almost always safe. Someone might still try to attack you while you rest and sleep, but it isn't the same as sleeping in the wilderness, where a beast could show up at any moment. A town with a lot of unrest might not be safe. The GM has the final say.

When you complete a Rest, you remove all the damage you took and you regain all your Rally Points. If you have Wounds, roll a Body Check for your Body Wounds and a Mind Check for your Mind Wounds. Each check removes Wounds of its own type only (Body Check → Body Wounds; Mind Check → Mind Wounds).

Roll Result
Tier 1 You remove 1 Wound.
Tier 2 You remove 2 Wounds.
Tier 3 You remove 3 Wounds.

Health States

Bloodied

You are Bloodied while your Vigor damage is equal to or more than your Vigor. It has no effect by itself: Actions and features use it, such as "when an ally becomes Bloodied" or "against a Bloodied target".

Strained

You are Strained while your Resolve damage is equal to or more than your Resolve. Like Bloodied, it has no effect by itself: Actions and features use it.

Every creature knows whether a creature it perceives is Bloodied or Strained: the GM says so when an NPC becomes either.

Designer's Tip

A feature that cares about an enemy being Bloodied or Strained usually says "when it becomes": an enemy is Bloodied for about a round before it goes Down, so "while" rarely matters. A rider on your own Action can say "while" ("if the target is Strained, heal 2 more").

Desperate

You are Down and still fighting. You are Slowed 1, or increase your Slowed value by 1 (to a maximum of 3), while Desperate.

  • If your Nonlethal damage reaches 50% of your Health Pool, you fall Unconscious.
  • If you take any Lethal damage, check your Dominant Damage and become Dying or Shattered.

Example: Health Pool 46, with 28 Lethal and 13 Nonlethal damage (5 damage away from Down). You take 5 Nonlethal damage and go Down with 18 Nonlethal, which is under 23 (50%). You choose to fight on as Desperate. You then take 5 more Nonlethal damage, reaching 23, and fall Unconscious. Your 28 Lethal damage and all conditions remain.

Dying

You are Slowed 1, or increase your Slowed value by 1 (to a maximum of 3), while Dying.

When you become Dying for the first time in an encounter, roll on the Dying Table. Then choose to collapse or keep fighting. If you become Dying again in the same encounter, don't roll: choose to collapse or keep fighting.

If you collapse, you are Unconscious. At the end of each of your turns, make a Body Check:

Roll Result
Tier 1 Roll on the Dying Table.
Tier 2 No effect.
Tier 3 You stabilize: roll on the Dying Table. You are no longer Dying, but you stay Unconscious.

If you keep fighting, at the end of each of your turns, make a Body Check:

Roll Result
Tier 1 Roll on the Dying Table.
Tier 2 No effect.
Tier 3 No effect.

After this check, you may choose to stop fighting and fall Unconscious.

If you take damage while you keep fighting, make a Body Check if it was Vigor damage, or a Mind Check if it was Resolve damage:

Roll Result
Tier 1 Roll on the Dying Table.
Tier 2 Roll on the Dying Table.
Tier 3 No effect.

After the check, you may choose to collapse and fall Unconscious.

Shattered

You are Slowed 1, or increase your Slowed value by 1 (to a maximum of 3), while Shattered.

When you become Shattered for the first time in an encounter, roll on the Shattered Table. Then choose to give up or keep fighting. If you become Shattered again in the same encounter, don't roll: choose to give up or keep fighting.

If you give up, you are Unconscious. At the end of each of your turns, make a Mind Check:

Roll Result
Tier 1 Roll on the Shattered Table.
Tier 2 No effect.
Tier 3 You stabilize: roll on the Shattered Table. You are no longer Shattered, but you stay Unconscious.

If you keep fighting, at the end of each of your turns, make a Mind Check:

Roll Result
Tier 1 Roll on the Shattered Table.
Tier 2 No effect.
Tier 3 No effect.

After this check, you may choose to stop fighting and fall Unconscious.

If you take damage while you keep fighting, make a Body Check if it was Vigor damage, or a Mind Check if it was Resolve damage:

Roll Result
Tier 1 Roll on the Shattered Table.
Tier 2 Roll on the Shattered Table.
Tier 3 No effect.

After the check, you may choose to give up and fall Unconscious.

Unconscious

  • You can't take Actions, you are Prone, and you drop everything you hold.
  • You can't be Engaged, and you threaten no one (see Flanking).
  • While Unconscious, every creature is Unsensed to you.
  • All your Rolls are Doomed, whatever the Attribute. The only exceptions are the Checks you roll each turn while Dying (Body) or Shattered (Mind); those are not Doomed.
  • Unless you are Down, a creature can wake you with the Interact Action (1A).
  • You can't wake up while Dying or Shattered, or while your damage is equal to or more than your Health Pool.
  • While Unconscious and not Dying nor Shattered, every hour you remove damage equal to what one of your Rally Points removes.
  • If you take damage while Down, you roll on the Dying or Shattered Table. If you weren't Dying or Shattered yet, check your Dominant Damage first and become one of them.

An Unconscious creature isn't a threat, so creatures normally don't attack them, even mindless ones (some very cruel creatures might). A creature that keeps fighting while Dying or Shattered is still a threat, and is attacked like anyone else.

Part II: Characters

Chapter 5: Characters

Building a Character

  1. Attributes. All four Attributes (Body, Mind, Appeal, Instinct) start at 0.
  2. Species. Apply your species' Attribute changes (the species are in the Species document). It also gives you a Vigor and a Resolve bonus, a Speed, your Reach (1), your Steadiness and your Size (all current species are Medium (3)).
  3. Class. Apply your class' Attribute increases. It also gives you a high and a low Health value (and the steps they grow by at each Stage), a Rally value, a Speed Modifier, a Weapon Modifier and a Power Modifier. Your Speed is your species' Speed plus your class' Speed Modifier.
  4. Choices. When a species or class says "or", pick one. A class's choices between two Attributes must be different from each other (see Distinct Choices). If your class lets you, choose which of its two Modifier values is your Weapon Modifier and which your Power Modifier (see Weapon, Power and Signature Modifiers).
  5. Health Pool. Assign your class's high Health value to Vigor or to Resolve and the low one to the other, then add your species' bonuses (neither can be under a third of the total). Your Health Pool is the two added together.
  6. Rally Points = your class' Rally value + 1 (it grows with your Stage).
  7. Level 1. Take what your class's level list gives at level 1: its Features, its Hallmark Action and Hallmark Reaction (a choice of two each), an Art, and your Escalation 2 ability (see Leveling Up). Weapons and armor are in the Gear document.

Classes

Your class gives you Attribute increases, a high and a low Health value with their Stage steps (used for your Health Pool), a Rally value (used for Rally Points), a Speed Modifier, a Weapon Modifier and a Power Modifier, an Armor Training, and a list of Escalation abilities.

When you pick your class, you choose its Attribute increases when they say "or", and the order of its Modifiers if it lets you. The Attribute choices can't be changed later; the rest can, for a while (see Swapping on a Rest).

Each class is written in its own document: Paladin and Archer.

Class Actions, Picks and the Repertoire

Over its first levels, every class gives you the same kinds of things:

  • A Hallmark Action: a choice of two Actions that are the class's fantasy; you take one, and the other is not yours. A Hallmark Action doesn't need the Signature trait: that trait only sets the Modifier an Action rolls.
  • A Hallmark Reaction: a choice of two Reactions, the same way.
  • An Art: a small Action with three Modes (see Reading an Action), for the things that are neither damage nor healing (at most a Modifier's damage, as Trick Shots). A class offers three; you take one at level 1 and a second at level 3.
  • An Encounter Pick.
  • The Escalation abilities: one for each of Escalation 2, 4 and 6, then the Apex (see Escalation Abilities).
  • Its Features.

A class's Class Actions are the Actions it gives you at level 1, the Hallmark Action and the Hallmark Reaction among them. Its Repertoire is everything else it offers, listed by Frequency: Passive (it works on its own), Turn, Round, Encounter and Daily. A Pick is one choice from the Repertoire: the level list says how many Picks you take at each level and from which list (an Encounter Pick comes from the Encounter list; a Pick "from any list" can come from any of them). Two classes' lists don't need to match: each offers what fits it.

Leveling Up

Each class has a level list: what you gain at each level (Features, Class Actions, Picks and Escalation abilities). When you reach a new level, you take what its entry gives you. Levels give options; Stages change the numbers (below).

The first three levels have the same shape for every class:

Level You gain
1 Your class's Features, a Hallmark Action, a Hallmark Reaction, an Art, your Escalation 2 ability, a Skill Talent
2 Your class's Escalation hook, an Encounter Pick, your Escalation 4 ability, a Talent
3 A second Art, your Escalation 6 ability, a Skill Talent
4 The Apex, a Stage Talent and the numbers of Stage 1

So a level 1 character's Escalation ability starts working at Escalation 2: round 2 of a fight, or from the start with Momentum.

Talents

A Talent is a feature any character can take, apart from their class. The level list has two kinds of slots: Talents and Skill Talents (for skills, out of combat), and a Stage Talent at the first level of Stages 1, 2 and 3.

To be decided

The Talents are set aside for now: none is in the book while the first three levels of the classes are finished. Every Talent slot stays empty until they are written again (the Skill Talents come with the Skills rules).

Swapping on a Rest

When you complete a Rest, you can change any of the choices your class's level list gave you: your Hallmark Action, your Hallmark Reaction, your Arts, your Picks, your Escalation abilities and your Talents. Each new choice must be one you could have made at that level.

During Stage 0 you can also swap the order of your Modifiers on a Rest, if your class lets you choose it. From Stage 1 on, that order and the Modifier you raise at Stage 1 are permanent.

Optional rule. If the GM allows it, on a Rest you can also change your class's Attribute choices and which of its two Health values is your Vigor.

Stages

The levels are grouped in Stages: Stage 0 is levels 1 to 3, Stage 1 levels 4 to 7, Stage 2 levels 8 to 11 and Stage 3 levels 12 to 15. Your numbers change only when you reach a new Stage, and the NPCs of the Bestiary follow them (their tables are written by Stage).

Stage 0 (levels 1-3) Stage 1 (levels 4-7) Stage 2 (levels 8-11) Stage 3 (levels 12-15)
Modifiers your class's values (+2 and +1) +1 to your Weapon or Power Modifier +1 to your Weapon and Power Modifiers
Health your class's values + your class's Stage 1 steps + your class's Stage 2 steps + your class's Stage 3 steps
Guard per unspent AP 2 2 3 4
Rally Points Rally + 1 Rally + 2 Rally + 3 Rally + 4
Stage Talent at level 4 at level 8 at level 12

Your Attributes don't grow with your level or your Stage. A Modifier is never above +4.

To be decided

Only Stage 0 is written so far: the classes' levels 4 and above, their Health steps for Stages 1, 2 and 3, and the Bestiary's later tables come after it.

Distinct Choices

When your class gives you a choice between two Attributes, you can't pick an Attribute you already picked from another of its choices: each Attribute increase goes to a different Attribute. If a class offers "Body or Appeal +1" and "Appeal or Instinct +1" and you pick Appeal for the first, you must pick Instinct for the second.

Weapon, Power and Signature Modifiers

Your class gives you two Modifier values: +2 and +1 at level 1. One is your Weapon Modifier, which Weapon Actions roll; the other is your Power Modifier, which Power Actions roll and which sets your Ward Defense. Your class says which is which, or lets you choose. They don't come from your Attributes, and your Attributes don't change them.

They grow with your Stage: at Stage 1 (level 4) add +1 to the one you choose, at Stage 3 (level 12) +1 to both. A Modifier is never above +4.

Your Signature Modifier is the higher of your Weapon Modifier and your Power Modifier (if they are equal, choose one). Actions with the Signature trait roll it.

Your Attributes set your Checks (Initiative is one), your Saves, your Defenses against an Attribute, your rolls on the Dying and Shattered Tables and the Attribute Actions, such as Shove and Trip (see Rolls).

Example

Lonny's Paladin has Weapon Modifier +1 and Power Modifier +2 (Ward Defense 13; his Signature Modifier is +2, from his Power Modifier). At level 4 he adds +1 to his Weapon Modifier: +2 / +2. At level 12 both rise: +3 / +3.

Escalation Abilities

Each class has a list of Escalation abilities, two for each of Escalation 2, 4 and 6, and Apex Actions, the class's big Encounter Action that needs Escalation 6. An Escalation ability is a Passive, which works while your Escalation is at least the number on its card, or an Action that you can use only while your Escalation is at least that number. You choose one for each of Escalation 2, 4 and 6: the Escalation 2 one at level 1, the Escalation 4 one at level 2 and the Escalation 6 one at level 3. You choose your Apex at level 4. Nothing spends Escalation. See Escalation for how it rises.

Part III: Reference
